questions.stem: (a) Explain briefly how each of the following factors can be used to differentiate a subsistence farmer from a commercial farmer. (i) Land use [3 marks] (ii) Finance [3 marks] (iii) Illiteracy [3 marks] (iv) Labour [3 marks] (b) State four reasons why farming is generally not an attractive business to the youths. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Land use: subsistence farmer cultivates small, often fragmented holdings (usually under 2 ha) mostly inherited; commercial farmer uses large expanses of land, often bought or leased
3 marks: (a)(ii) Finance: subsistence farmer has little capital, relies on personal savings/relatives and has no access to credit; commercial farmer has large capital and access to bank loans/credit
3 marks: (a)(iii) Illiteracy: subsistence farmers are mostly illiterate and slow to adopt innovations; commercial farmers are usually literate/educated and adopt new technologies readily
3 marks: (a)(iv) Labour: subsistence farmer uses family labour and crude tools; commercial farmer employs hired labour and machines
4 marks: (b) Any four (1 mark each): drudgery/hard manual work with crude tools; low income/profit; lack of capital and credit; difficulty in obtaining land; low social status/prestige of farming; lack of social amenities in rural areas; long gestation period before returns; risks from pests, diseases and weather
questions.explanation: (a) Land use: the subsistence farmer cultivates small, scattered, inherited plots, whereas the commercial farmer uses large areas, often bought or leased. Finance: the subsistence farmer has little capital and no access to credit, while the commercial farmer has large capital and can borrow from banks. Illiteracy: subsistence farmers are mostly illiterate and slow to adopt innovations; commercial farmers are educated and adopt technology quickly. Labour: the subsistence farmer uses family labour with crude tools; the commercial farmer uses hired labour and machines. (b) Farming is unattractive to youths because of drudgery, low income, lack of capital and land, low social status, poor rural amenities and high risk.

questions.stem: (a) List five tillage implements. [5 marks] (b) Describe two tillage operations in a mechanized farm. [6 marks] (c) State five ways of maintaining farm machinery. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) Any five (1 mark each): disc plough; mouldboard plough; disc harrow; spike-tooth/spring-tine harrow; ridger; rotary tiller (rotavator); sub-soiler; cultivator
3 marks: (b) First operation, e.g. ploughing - a tractor-drawn plough cuts, lifts and inverts the soil, burying weeds and trash and loosening the soil (primary tillage)
3 marks: (b) Second operation, e.g. harrowing - a harrow breaks the clods left after ploughing into a fine tilth and levels the seedbed (or ridging: a ridger forms ridges after harrowing)
5 marks: (c) Any five (1 mark each): clean after use; lubricate/grease moving parts; check and top up oil, water and battery; check tyre pressure; tighten loose nuts and bolts; replace worn-out parts; store under shelter; service at regular intervals; follow manufacturer's manual; use trained operators
questions.explanation: (a) Disc plough, mouldboard plough, disc harrow, spring-tine harrow, ridger (also rotavator, sub-soiler). (b) Ploughing: a tractor-drawn plough cuts and turns the soil to a depth, burying weeds and loosening it. Harrowing: a disc or tine harrow then breaks the large clods into a fine tilth and levels the seedbed; ridging follows where ridges are needed. (c) Clean machines after use, oil and grease moving parts, check fuel/oil/water levels and tyre pressure, tighten bolts and replace worn parts, house them under a shed and service regularly.

questions.topic: Types, composition and properties of soil
questions.stem: (a) Mention four components of a fertile soil. [2 marks] (b) In a tabular form, compare the (i) physical; [10 marks] (ii) chemical; [4 marks] properties of sand and clay.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Mineral matter; organic matter (humus); soil water; soil air (also soil organisms) (half a mark each, rounded)
2 marks: (b)(i) Particle size: sand is coarse (2.0 - 0.02 mm); clay is very fine (less than 0.002 mm)
2 marks: Texture/feel: sand is gritty; clay is smooth and sticky when wet
2 marks: Water-holding capacity: sand is low; clay is high
2 marks: Drainage/aeration: sand is well drained and well aerated; clay is poorly drained and poorly aerated (easily waterlogged)
2 marks: Workability/plasticity/porosity: sand is light and easy to till, non-plastic, with large pore spaces; clay is heavy, plastic, with small pores and cracks when dry
2 marks: (b)(ii) Nutrient content/cation exchange capacity: sand is low; clay is high
2 marks: Leaching/chemical activity: sand is easily leached and chemically inactive; clay retains nutrients, is chemically active (colloidal) and is less easily leached
questions.explanation: (a) A fertile soil contains mineral particles, organic matter (humus), water and air, with living organisms. (b) Physical: sand particles are coarse and gritty, clay particles very fine and sticky; sand holds little water but drains and aerates well, while clay holds much water, drains poorly and waterlogs; sand is light and easy to work, clay is heavy and plastic when wet and cracks when dry. Chemical: clay has a high cation exchange capacity and high nutrient content and retains nutrients; sand has a low CEC, is low in nutrients and is easily leached.

questions.stem: (a) State four factors which influence nutrients availability to crops. [4 marks] (b) Explain briefly the effects of three of the factors listed in (a) on the availability of nutrients to plants. [9 marks] (c) List three methods of replacing lost nutrients in the soil. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Any four (1 mark each): soil pH; leaching; erosion; crop removal (harvesting); burning; soil texture; organic matter content; soil microorganisms; soil water/moisture
3 marks: (b) First factor explained, e.g. soil pH - very acidic or very alkaline soils make nutrients such as P unavailable (fixed) while some micronutrients may become toxic; most nutrients are available near neutral pH
3 marks: (b) Second factor explained, e.g. leaching - heavy rainfall washes soluble nutrients below the root zone, making them unavailable
3 marks: (b) Third factor explained, e.g. erosion - removes the nutrient-rich topsoil; or crop removal - nutrients are taken away in harvested produce
3 marks: (c) Any three (1 mark each): application of organic manures/compost; application of inorganic fertilizers; crop rotation/planting of legumes; bush fallowing; cover cropping; liming; mulching
questions.explanation: (a) Soil pH, leaching, erosion and crop removal (also burning, texture, organic matter, micro-organisms). (b) Soil pH: extremes of acidity or alkalinity fix nutrients such as phosphorus in insoluble forms, so most nutrients are best available near neutral pH. Leaching: heavy rain washes soluble nutrients such as nitrates beyond the root zone. Erosion: wind or water removes the fertile topsoil that holds most of the nutrients. (c) Nutrients can be replaced by adding organic manure or inorganic fertilizers, by crop rotation with legumes and by bush fallowing.

questions.stem: Describe the cultivation of maize under the following headings: (a) Land preparation; [2 marks] (b) Propagation; [1 mark] (c) Planting date; [2 marks] (d) Seed rate; [1 mark] (e) Spacing; [1 mark] (f) Fertilizer requirement; [2 marks] (g) Weeding; [1 mark] (h) Harvesting; [3 marks] (i) Storage. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Clear the land, plough and harrow (or make ridges/mounds) to give a fine tilth
1 mark: (b) Propagated by seeds (grains), sown directly 2 - 3 per hole at 2.5 - 5 cm depth
2 marks: (c) Early season: March - April (onset of rains in the south); late season: August - September (May - June in the savanna)
1 mark: (d) Seed rate of about 20 - 25 kg per hectare
1 mark: (e) Spacing of about 75 - 90 cm x 25 - 30 cm (e.g. 90 cm x 30 cm, or 75 cm x 25 cm at one plant per stand)
2 marks: (f) NPK 15:15:15 at about 200 - 300 kg/ha at planting, followed by side-dressing with nitrogen (e.g. urea or sulphate of ammonia) about 4 - 6 weeks after planting
1 mark: (g) Weed 2 - 3 times manually (e.g. 3 and 6 weeks after planting) or use pre-emergence herbicide
3 marks: (h) Green maize harvested about 70 - 90 days after planting when the silk turns brown; dry grain harvested at about 100 - 120 days when the husks dry; harvested by hand-plucking the cobs (or combine harvester)
3 marks: (i) Dry the cobs/grains to about 12 - 13% moisture; shell and store in clean, dry, well-aerated cribs, silos or bags; treat with insecticide (e.g. actellic) against weevils
questions.explanation: Land is cleared, ploughed and harrowed (or ridged). Maize is propagated by seed, 2 - 3 seeds per hole. The early crop is planted in March - April and the late crop in August - September in the south. The seed rate is about 20 - 25 kg/ha at a spacing of about 75 - 90 cm x 25 - 30 cm. Apply NPK at planting and side-dress with nitrogen at 4 - 6 weeks. Weed two or three times. Green maize is harvested at 70 - 90 days and dry maize at 100 - 120 days when the husks are brown and dry. The grain is dried to about 12% moisture, treated with insecticide and stored in cribs, silos or bags.

questions.stem: State the causal organism, mode of transmission and control measures of any four of the following diseases. (a) Tikka [4 marks] (b) Groundnut rosette [4 marks] (c) Cocoa blackpod [4 marks] (d) Cassava mosaic [4 marks] (e) Angular leaf spot [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Tikka (leaf spot of groundnut): causal organism - fungus Cercospora arachidicola/C. personata; transmission - wind-borne spores, rain splash and infected crop debris; control - crop rotation, destroying infected debris, resistant varieties, fungicide spray (e.g. Bordeaux mixture, benomyl)
4 marks: (b) Groundnut rosette: causal organism - virus; transmission - aphids (Aphis craccivora); control - early planting at close spacing, insecticide spray against aphids, uprooting and burning infected plants, resistant varieties
4 marks: (c) Cocoa blackpod: causal organism - fungus Phytophthora palmivora (megakarya); transmission - rain splash, wind, insects, infected pods and soil; control - remove and destroy infected pods, regular harvesting, reduce shade and humidity, spray copper fungicides
4 marks: (d) Cassava mosaic: causal organism - virus; transmission - whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) and infected cuttings; control - use disease-free cuttings, resistant varieties, uproot and burn infected plants, control whitefly with insecticides
questions.explanation: Tikka: fungus (Cercospora spp.), spread by wind and rain splash and infected debris; controlled by rotation, field sanitation, resistant varieties and fungicides. Groundnut rosette: virus transmitted by aphids; controlled by early, dense planting, insecticide sprays, rogueing and resistant varieties. Cocoa black pod: fungus Phytophthora palmivora, spread by rain splash, insects and infected pods; controlled by removing infected pods, frequent harvesting, shade regulation and copper fungicides. Cassava mosaic: virus spread by whitefly and infected cuttings; controlled by clean planting material, resistant varieties, rogueing and vector control. (Angular leaf spot of cotton/beans - bacterium Xanthomonas, seed-borne and rain splash; control by seed dressing, resistant varieties and rotation - may be chosen instead.)

questions.stem: (a) Enumerate six problems militating against rabbit production in West Africa. [6 marks] (b)(i) Name four common diseases of rabbits. [4 marks] (ii) Discuss briefly two of the following diseases: Enteritis, Bloat and Helminthiasis under the headings below: I - causative agent; [2 marks] II - symptoms; [2 marks] III - control. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) Any six (1 mark each): high cost of feed/concentrates; diseases and parasites; lack of improved breeds; inadequate capital/credit; poor housing; predators and thieves; lack of technical knowledge/extension; poor marketing and low acceptance of rabbit meat; heat stress; high mortality of young
4 marks: (b)(i) Any four (1 mark each): coccidiosis; enteritis (diarrhoea); bloat; snuffles (pasteurellosis); pneumonia; ear canker (mange); mastitis; helminthiasis
2 marks: (b)(ii) I. Causative agents, e.g. enteritis - bacteria (E. coli) or poor feeding/sudden change of diet; bloat - feeding on wet/lush green or fermentable feed; helminthiasis - worms (roundworms, tapeworms)
2 marks: II. Symptoms, e.g. enteritis - diarrhoea, dehydration, loss of appetite and weight; bloat - swollen distended abdomen, difficult breathing, grinding of teeth; helminthiasis - emaciation, rough coat, pot belly, anaemia, diarrhoea
2 marks: III. Control, e.g. enteritis - hygiene, avoid sudden feed changes, antibiotics; bloat - avoid wet/lush feeds, give dry roughage, drench with oil; helminthiasis - regular deworming with anthelmintics, clean hutches and feed
questions.explanation: (a) Problems include high cost of feed, diseases and parasites, lack of improved breeds, inadequate capital, predators and thieves, lack of technical know-how and poor market acceptance of rabbit meat. (b) Common diseases: coccidiosis, enteritis, bloat, snuffles, ear mange, pneumonia. Enteritis is caused by bacteria or wrong feeding, shows as diarrhoea and weight loss, and is controlled by hygiene, gradual diet changes and antibiotics. Bloat is caused by wet or lush fermentable feeds, shows as a swollen abdomen and laboured breathing, and is controlled by feeding dry roughage and avoiding wet greens. Helminthiasis is caused by worms, shows as emaciation, pot-belly and rough coat, and is controlled by regular deworming and sanitation.

questions.stem: (a) State four advantages of siting a fish pond in the savannah area. [4 marks] (b) State and explain briefly six conditions which must be avoided in the siting of a fish pond. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Any four (1 mark each): land is relatively flat and easy to clear and construct; land is cheaper and more available; abundant sunlight promotes plankton growth (natural fish food); warm temperature favours fast fish growth; fewer trees so less leaf fall and shading; provides fish protein in an area of scarce animal protein / uses water from dams and rivers for irrigation and fish
12 marks: (b) Any six conditions, each stated and explained (2 marks each): sandy/porous soil - water seeps away; land prone to flooding - fish escape and predators/wild fish enter; polluted water source (industrial/agricultural chemicals) - kills fish; steep slope/rocky land - costly construction and erosion; area far from a reliable water source - pond dries up; shaded area under trees - reduces sunlight for plankton and leaves foul water; acidic/swampy soil - poor water quality; area near busy roads/homes - theft and noise
questions.explanation: (a) In the savanna the land is flat and easy to clear, land is cheap, the sun and warm temperature promote plankton and rapid fish growth, and there are few trees to shade the pond or drop leaves. (b) Avoid sandy or porous soils that will not hold water; flood-prone sites where fish escape and predators enter; polluted water sources; steep or rocky land that is expensive to excavate; sites without a perennial water supply; heavily shaded sites; very acidic soils; and isolated places where theft is likely.

questions.stem: (a) Differentiate between marketing and marketing functions in agriculture. [4 marks] (b) Mention four characteristics of agricultural produce in relation to marketing. [4 marks] (c) List and explain briefly any four marketing functions in agriculture. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Marketing is all the activities involved in moving agricultural produce from the producer (farm) to the final consumer
2 marks: Marketing functions are the specific services/activities performed in the marketing process, e.g. assembling, grading, processing, storage, transportation, packaging, advertising and selling
4 marks: (b) Any four (1 mark each): perishable; bulky; seasonal in production; produced in small quantities by scattered farmers; variable in quality (not standardized); demand is relatively inelastic; prices fluctuate
8 marks: (c) Any four functions listed and explained (2 marks each): assembling - collecting produce from many farmers into one place; grading/standardization - sorting into classes by size and quality; processing - changing produce into more useful/durable forms; storage - keeping produce until it is needed, ensuring all-year supply; transportation - moving produce to where it is needed; packaging - putting produce in suitable containers; advertising/promotion; financing; risk bearing; selling/distribution
questions.explanation: (a) Marketing is the whole process of moving produce from the farm gate to the consumer, while marketing functions are the individual activities carried out in that process. (b) Farm produce is perishable, bulky, seasonal, of variable quality and produced in small quantities by scattered farmers. (c) Assembling collects produce from many farmers; grading sorts it by quality to fetch fair prices; processing converts it into more durable or useful forms; storage preserves it for sale out of season; transportation moves it to markets (also packaging, advertising, financing and risk bearing).

questions.stem: (a) Mention four desirable qualities of a farm manager. [4 marks] (b) State four problems that can be encountered by a farm manager. [6 marks] (c) Write short notes on the following: (i) farm assets, [3 marks] (ii) farm income statement. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Any four (1 mark each): good technical knowledge of farming; honesty and integrity; good leadership and ability to relate with workers; hard-working and dedicated; ability to plan and take decisions; ability to keep records; good health; innovativeness/readiness to take risks
6 marks: (b) Any four (1.5 marks each): inadequate capital/credit; shortage of skilled labour; pests and diseases; unfavourable weather/natural hazards; poor marketing and price fluctuations; lack of storage and processing facilities; government policy changes; land tenure problems
3 marks: (c)(i) Farm assets are the things of value owned by the farm business, e.g. land, buildings, machinery, livestock, crops in store, cash and debts owed to the farm; they are fixed (long-term) or current (short-term)
3 marks: (c)(ii) A farm income statement (profit and loss account) records all the farm's receipts (income) and expenses over a period (usually a year) to show the net farm income - profit or loss
questions.explanation: (a) A farm manager should be knowledgeable, honest, hard-working, a good leader and decision-maker who keeps proper records. (b) Problems include inadequate capital, shortage of skilled labour, pests and diseases, bad weather, poor marketing and fluctuating prices, and lack of storage facilities. (c) Farm assets are everything of value owned by the farm - fixed assets like land, buildings and machinery, and current assets like cash, stock and produce. A farm income statement summarises all receipts and expenses over an accounting period to show whether the farm made a profit or a loss.

questions.stem: (a) State four merits of each of the following: (i) agriculture; (ii) forestry; (iii) wildlife conservation. [12 marks] (b) List four non-agricultural uses of land. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a)(i) Agriculture, any four (1 mark each): provides food; provides raw materials for industries; source of employment; earns foreign exchange; source of income/revenue; provides shelter/clothing materials
4 marks: (a)(ii) Forestry, any four (1 mark each): provides timber and wood for building/furniture; fuel wood; habitat for wildlife; prevents erosion/protects watersheds; acts as windbreak; source of medicinal plants, gums, latex; regulates climate/adds organic matter; tourism
4 marks: (a)(iii) Wildlife conservation, any four (1 mark each): preserves animal species from extinction; tourism/recreation; source of foreign exchange and revenue; source of game meat (bush meat) and animal products; research and education; employment (game wardens)
4 marks: (b) Any four (1 mark each): building/housing; road and rail construction; industries/factories; mining; recreation (parks, stadia); schools/hospitals; airports
questions.explanation: (a) Agriculture provides food, industrial raw materials, employment and foreign exchange. Forestry supplies timber and fuel wood, protects the soil from erosion, acts as a windbreak and shelters wildlife. Wildlife conservation prevents extinction of species, promotes tourism and foreign exchange, supplies game meat and provides opportunities for research and education. (b) Land is also used for housing, roads/railways, industries, mining and recreation.

questions.stem: (a) Describe briefly four types of individual land tenure systems. [8 marks] (b) List four advantages and four disadvantages of the land use act. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
8 marks: (a) Any four described (2 marks each): inheritance - land passed from parents to children; purchase/outright ownership (freehold) - land bought and owned permanently; leasehold/rent - land used for a fixed period on payment; gift - land given free by an individual; pledge - land given as security for a loan, used by the creditor until repaid; tenancy/share cropping
4 marks: (b) Advantages, any four (1 mark each): land is vested in government, making land available for development/agriculture; reduces land disputes and litigation; prevents land speculation; allows large-scale farming; encourages security of tenure via certificate of occupancy; checks fragmentation
4 marks: (b) Disadvantages, any four (1 mark each): bureaucracy in obtaining certificate of occupancy; corruption/favouritism by officials; land owners lose ownership/rights; inadequate compensation; land can be revoked by government; discourages long-term investment by communities
questions.explanation: (a) Inheritance: land passes from parents to children; purchase: land bought outright and owned permanently; lease/rent: land used for an agreed period on payment; gift: land freely given; pledge: land used by a creditor until a loan is repaid. (b) The Land Use Act makes land available to government and investors for development, reduces disputes and speculation and permits large-scale farming. However, obtaining the certificate of occupancy is slow and bureaucratic, officials may be corrupt, original owners lose their rights and compensation is inadequate.

questions.stem: (a) Discuss three effects of each of the following factors on crop production: (i) water; (ii) air; (iii) soil microbes. [9 marks] (b) List three edaphic and four climatic factors that affect crop productivity. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Water (1 mark each, any three): needed for photosynthesis; solvent for nutrient uptake and transport; maintains turgidity; needed for germination; cools the plant through transpiration; excess causes waterlogging
3 marks: (a)(ii) Air (1 mark each, any three): supplies CO2 for photosynthesis; supplies O2 for root and seed respiration/germination; nitrogen fixed by microbes; air movement aids pollination/seed dispersal; strong wind causes lodging
3 marks: (a)(iii) Soil microbes (1 mark each, any three): decompose organic matter to humus/release nutrients; fix atmospheric nitrogen (Rhizobium); improve soil structure; some cause plant diseases; nitrification
3 marks: (b) Edaphic, any three (1 mark each): soil pH; soil texture; soil structure; soil fertility/nutrients; soil water; soil air; soil temperature; topography
4 marks: (b) Climatic, any four (1 mark each): rainfall; temperature; light/sunshine; relative humidity; wind
questions.explanation: (a) Water is a raw material for photosynthesis, dissolves and transports nutrients, keeps cells turgid and is needed for germination. Air supplies CO2 for photosynthesis and O2 for root respiration and germination, and wind aids pollination though strong winds cause lodging. Soil microbes decompose organic matter releasing nutrients, fix atmospheric nitrogen and improve soil structure, but some cause diseases. (b) Edaphic: soil pH, texture, fertility. Climatic: rainfall, temperature, light, relative humidity.

questions.stem: (a) Explain briefly the processes of formation of (i) igneous rocks; (ii) sedimentary rocks; (iii) metamorphic rocks. [9 marks] (b) Give two examples of each of igneous and metamorphic rocks and three examples of sedimentary rocks. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Igneous rocks are formed by the cooling and solidification of molten magma, either inside the earth (intrusive, e.g. granite) or on the surface as lava (extrusive, e.g. basalt)
3 marks: (a)(ii) Sedimentary rocks are formed from fragments of other rocks/organic remains deposited in layers (usually under water) and compacted and cemented over a long time
3 marks: (a)(iii) Metamorphic rocks are formed when existing igneous or sedimentary rocks are changed by great heat and/or pressure
2 marks: (b) Igneous: any two of granite, basalt, gabbro, diorite, dolerite
2 marks: (b) Metamorphic: any two of marble, quartzite, slate, gneiss, schist
3 marks: (b) Sedimentary: any three of sandstone, limestone, shale, clay, conglomerate, coal, chalk
questions.explanation: (a) Igneous rocks form when magma cools and solidifies, inside the crust (intrusive) or at the surface as lava (extrusive). Sedimentary rocks form from layers of sediments - rock fragments, plant and animal remains - deposited and compacted/cemented over time. Metamorphic rocks form when igneous or sedimentary rocks are altered by heat and pressure. (b) Igneous: granite, basalt. Metamorphic: marble, quartzite (also slate, gneiss). Sedimentary: sandstone, limestone, shale.

questions.stem: Explain pasture management practices under the following sub-headings: (a) land preparation; [3 marks] (b) three methods of propagation; [3 marks] (c) two methods of sowing; [2 marks] (d) fertilizer application; [1 mark] (e) grazing; [3 marks] (f) four management practices other than fertilizing and grazing. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Clear the land of bush/trees, plough and harrow to a fine tilth (stump and remove debris)
3 marks: (b) Seeds; stem cuttings (stolons/runners); root splits/crown splits (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) Broadcasting; drilling in rows (1 mark each)
1 mark: (d) Apply nitrogenous/NPK fertilizer or farmyard manure at establishment and after grazing to boost regrowth
3 marks: (e) Practise rotational grazing (paddocking); avoid overgrazing by matching stocking rate to carrying capacity; allow rest periods for regrowth
4 marks: (f) Any four (1 mark each): weed control; pest and disease control; irrigation; reseeding/gap filling; topping/mowing; mixing grasses with legumes; fire control (fire tracing); conserving excess as hay/silage
questions.explanation: (a) The land is cleared, ploughed and harrowed to a fine tilth. (b) Pasture is propagated by seed, by stem cuttings (stolons/runners) and by root/crown splits. (c) Seed is broadcast or drilled in rows. (d) Fertilizer or manure is applied at establishment and after grazing. (e) Rotational grazing with proper stocking rates prevents overgrazing and allows regrowth. (f) Other practices include weeding, pest control, irrigation, reseeding, mowing, legume introduction, fire control and conservation of excess forage as hay or silage.

questions.stem: Give an account of the production of banana, using the following sub-headings: (a) one common variety; [1 mark] (b) planting materials; [2 marks] (c) propagation; [3 marks] (d) husbandry; [3 marks] (e) two common pests; [2 marks] (f) two common diseases and how each is controlled; [4 marks] (g) maturity period. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Any one variety, e.g. Dwarf Cavendish, Gros Michel, Lacatan, Robusta, Giant Cavendish
2 marks: (b) Suckers (sword suckers/water suckers) and corms (bits)
3 marks: (c) Vegetative propagation: suckers are separated from the mother plant, trimmed and planted in holes about 60 cm x 60 cm x 60 cm at a spacing of about 3 m x 3 m, at the beginning of the rains
3 marks: (d) Weeding (manual/herbicide); application of manure/fertilizer (NPK/potash); mulching; desuckering (leaving 2 - 3 followers); propping of plants bearing bunches; removing dead leaves
2 marks: (e) Banana weevil (Cosmopolites sordidus); nematodes (also thrips, aphids)
2 marks: (f) First disease and control, e.g. Sigatoka leaf spot (fungal) - spray fungicides, remove infected leaves, good drainage
2 marks: (f) Second disease and control, e.g. Panama disease (Fusarium wilt) - resistant varieties, uproot and burn infected plants, use clean suckers; or bunchy top (virus) - control aphids, rogueing
1 mark: (g) About 12 - 15 months after planting (bunch ready about 3 - 4 months after flowering)
questions.explanation: Variety: Dwarf Cavendish (or Gros Michel). Planting materials are sword suckers or corms. Suckers are removed from the mother plant, trimmed and planted in large holes at about 3 m x 3 m at the start of the rains. Husbandry involves weeding, mulching, manuring (especially potash), desuckering to 2 - 3 followers and propping plants with bunches. Pests: banana weevil and nematodes. Diseases: Sigatoka leaf spot, controlled with fungicides and removal of infected leaves; Panama disease, controlled with resistant varieties, clean suckers and destroying infected plants. Banana matures in about 12 - 15 months.

questions.stem: (a) Write short notes on the following: (i) maintenance ration; (ii) production ration; (iii) balanced ration; (iv) malnutrition. [8 marks] (b) Mention four factors normally considered when deciding the type of feed an animal should be placed on. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Maintenance ration is the amount of feed required by an animal to keep its body functions going (basal metabolism) without gaining or losing weight or producing anything
2 marks: (a)(ii) Production ration is the feed given in addition to the maintenance ration for production purposes such as growth, milk, eggs, wool, work or pregnancy
2 marks: (a)(iii) A balanced ration is one that contains all the nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water) in the right proportions and quantities for the animal's needs
2 marks: (a)(iv) Malnutrition is a condition resulting from feeding an animal a diet lacking in one or more nutrients, or containing them in wrong proportions (under- or over-nutrition)
8 marks: (b) Any four (2 marks each): type/species of animal (ruminant or non-ruminant); age of the animal; purpose of production (meat, milk, eggs, work); physiological state (pregnancy, lactation); size/body weight; health condition; cost and availability of feed; palatability/digestibility of feed
questions.explanation: (a) A maintenance ration keeps the animal's vital functions going without weight change; a production ration is the extra feed for growth, milk, eggs, work or pregnancy; a balanced ration supplies all nutrients in correct proportions; malnutrition results from diets deficient in or with wrong proportions of nutrients. (b) Feed type is chosen according to the species (ruminant or monogastric), age, purpose of production, physiological state (e.g. pregnancy/lactation), health, and cost and availability of feedstuffs.

questions.topic: Anatomy and physiology of farm animals
questions.stem: (a) Describe with the aid of a diagram the stomach of a named ruminant. [13 marks] (b) State three functions of the first compartment of the stomach of a ruminant. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Named ruminant, e.g. cow (goat, sheep)
4 marks: Diagram correctly showing and labelling the four compartments - rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum - with oesophagus and duodenum (1 mark each compartment)
2 marks: Rumen - the largest compartment (paunch); stores and ferments food with micro-organisms that digest cellulose
2 marks: Reticulum - honeycomb-like lining; traps foreign bodies and forms the bolus (cud) for regurgitation
2 marks: Omasum - many leaf-like folds (manyplies); grinds food and absorbs water
2 marks: Abomasum - the true (glandular) stomach; secretes gastric juice/enzymes for digestion of protein
3 marks: (b) Functions of the rumen, any three (1 mark each): storage of large quantities of food; microbial fermentation/digestion of cellulose; synthesis of vitamin B complex and microbial protein; production and absorption of volatile fatty acids; softening/mixing of food
questions.explanation: In a cow, the stomach has four compartments. The rumen (paunch), the largest, stores and ferments food with microbes that digest cellulose. The reticulum, with a honeycomb lining, traps foreign bodies and forms the cud for rechewing. The omasum has leaf-like folds that grind the food and absorb water. The abomasum is the true glandular stomach which secretes gastric juice. The diagram shows oesophagus entering between rumen and reticulum, and the abomasum leading to the duodenum. (b) The rumen stores food, ferments cellulose by microbial action, synthesises B vitamins and microbial protein, and absorbs volatile fatty acids.

questions.stem: (a) Explain the following terms: (i) appreciation; [2 marks] (ii) depreciation; [2 marks] (iii) salvage value. [2 marks] (b) List two items on the farm which will normally appreciate in value. [2 marks] (c) A farmer bought a fairly used Fiat tractor for N12,000.00 in 1988. He later sold it for N3,000.00 in 1997 when he discovered that it was expensive to maintain. Find the tractor's: (i) salvage value; (ii) overall depreciation; (iii) annual depreciation. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Appreciation is the increase in the value of an asset over time
2 marks: (a)(ii) Depreciation is the loss (decrease) in the value of an asset over time due to wear and tear, age or obsolescence
2 marks: (a)(iii) Salvage (scrap) value is the value of an asset at the end of its useful life or when it is disposed of
2 marks: (b) Any two: land; buildings; growing livestock (young animals); tree crops/plantations
2 marks: (c)(i) Salvage value = N3,000.00
3 marks: (c)(ii) Overall depreciation = cost - salvage value = N12,000.00 - N3,000.00 = N9,000.00
3 marks: (c)(iii) Years of use = 1997 - 1988 = 9 years; annual depreciation = N9,000.00 / 9 = N1,000.00 per year
questions.explanation: (a) Appreciation is a rise in an asset's value; depreciation is a fall in value due to wear, age or obsolescence; salvage value is what the asset is worth when disposed of at the end of its use. (b) Land and buildings (also young livestock, tree crops) usually appreciate. (c) Salvage value = N3,000; overall depreciation = 12,000 - 3,000 = N9,000; over 9 years (1988 - 1997) annual depreciation = N1,000 per year (straight-line).

questions.stem: (a) Briefly explain (i) agricultural finance; [2 marks] (ii) agricultural credit. [2 marks] (b) Explain four significance of agricultural finance. [8 marks] (c) Mention one problem farmers encounter in obtaining credits from the following credit sources: (i) commercial banks; (ii) community banks; (iii) money lenders; (iv) family sources. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Agricultural finance is the study/provision of the money (capital) used in agricultural production - how funds are acquired, managed and used in farming
2 marks: (a)(ii) Agricultural credit is money (or inputs) borrowed by farmers from individuals or institutions for farming, to be repaid with or without interest at an agreed time
8 marks: (b) Any four explained (2 marks each): enables purchase of inputs (seeds, fertilizers, agrochemicals); allows expansion/large-scale production; enables adoption of new technology/mechanization; pays for labour; provides for storage, processing and marketing; helps farmers recover from losses/disasters; increases productivity, income and standard of living
1 mark: (c)(i) Commercial banks: demand collateral security / high interest rates / cumbersome procedures
1 mark: (c)(ii) Community banks: limited funds, so only small loans are available
1 mark: (c)(iii) Money lenders: charge exorbitant interest rates
1 mark: (c)(iv) Family sources: amounts are small and unreliable
questions.explanation: (a) Agricultural finance deals with acquiring and using money capital in farming; agricultural credit is money or inputs borrowed by farmers to be repaid later, usually with interest. (b) Finance enables farmers to buy inputs, expand their farms, adopt mechanization and new technology, pay labour, and fund storage, processing and marketing, thereby raising output and income. (c) Commercial banks demand collateral and charge high interest; community banks have limited funds; money lenders charge exorbitant interest; family sources give small, unreliable amounts.

questions.stem: (a) Define communal land tenure system. [2 marks] (b) State three advantages and five disadvantages of the communal land tenure system. [8 marks] (c) State two other land tenure systems in your country, giving one advantage and one disadvantage of each. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Communal land tenure is a system in which land belongs to the community (village, clan or family) and is held in trust by the chief/family head, who allocates it to members for use
3 marks: (b) Advantages, any three (1 mark each): every member has access to land; land disputes are minimal/settled by elders; land cannot be sold to strangers; no payment for land; promotes communal unity
5 marks: (b) Disadvantages, any five (1 mark each): leads to land fragmentation; insecurity of tenure discourages long-term investment/permanent crops; land cannot be used as collateral; large-scale/mechanized farming is difficult; may cause disputes over allocation; strangers find it hard to obtain land
3 marks: (c) First system, e.g. inheritance (1 mark), advantage - free access and security for family members (1 mark), disadvantage - fragmentation into small plots (1 mark)
3 marks: (c) Second system, e.g. leasehold/rent (1 mark), advantage - non-owners get access to land (1 mark), disadvantage - limited period/rent discourages long-term investment (1 mark); or purchase (freehold): advantage - permanent ownership/collateral; disadvantage - expensive
questions.explanation: (a) Under communal tenure, land is owned by the whole community or family and held in trust by the chief or family head, who allocates portions to members for use. (b) It gives every member access to land free of charge, prevents sale to outsiders and promotes unity; but it causes fragmentation, insecurity of tenure, prevents use of land as collateral, hinders mechanization and large-scale farming, and can lead to disputes. (c) Inheritance gives family members free land but fragments it; leasehold gives non-owners access but for a limited period, discouraging permanent improvements (purchase gives permanent ownership but is expensive).

questions.stem: (a) List and discuss five limitations of farm mechanisation. [10 marks] (b) State four ways by which farmers can be encouraged to adopt farm mechanisation. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: (a) Any five listed and discussed (2 marks each): small/fragmented farm holdings make machine use uneconomic; high cost of machines and spare parts beyond farmers' means; lack of skilled operators and mechanics; unsuitable topography/soil (hilly, swampy, stumps); illiteracy of farmers; land tenure problems; lack of spare parts and maintenance facilities; some crops (e.g. tree crops) are not easily mechanized; machines displace labour (unemployment)
6 marks: (b) Any four (1.5 marks each): provision of credit/loans; subsidizing machines and spare parts; establishing tractor hire services; training farmers/operators through extension; land reform to make large holdings available; encouraging co-operatives; local manufacture of simple machines
questions.explanation: (a) Mechanization is limited by small, fragmented holdings that make machines uneconomic; the high cost of machines and spare parts; lack of skilled operators and repair facilities; unsuitable terrain such as hilly or swampy land with stumps; farmers' illiteracy; and land tenure problems. (b) Farmers can be encouraged through credit facilities, subsidies on machinery, government tractor hire services, training by extension agents, land reform and formation of co-operatives.

questions.stem: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of each of the following farming practices: (a) overgrazing; (b) bush burning; (c) crop rotation; (d) mixed cropping. [16 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Overgrazing advantages: animals get plenty of feed in the short term / controls weeds and reduces fire hazard by keeping grass short / cheap feeding
2 marks: (a) Overgrazing disadvantages: exposes soil to erosion; destroys the pasture/reduces regrowth; compacts the soil; leads to desertification and spread of parasites
2 marks: (b) Bush burning advantages: cheap and fast land clearing; kills pests and disease organisms; ash adds potash/minerals; stimulates fresh regrowth of grass
2 marks: (b) Bush burning disadvantages: destroys organic matter and soil organisms; exposes soil to erosion; pollutes the air; may destroy property, wildlife and forest
2 marks: (c) Crop rotation advantages: maintains soil fertility; controls pests, diseases and weeds; makes efficient use of soil nutrients at different depths; reduces erosion
2 marks: (c) Crop rotation disadvantages: requires skill/knowledge to plan; may not suit land shortage/small holdings; a farmer may not grow his preferred crop every season
2 marks: (d) Mixed cropping advantages: insurance against total crop failure; better soil cover, reducing erosion; legumes improve fertility; higher total yield per unit area; provides varied food
2 marks: (d) Mixed cropping disadvantages: competition among crops for nutrients, water and light; difficult to mechanize; difficult to apply fertilizers/pesticides selectively; lower yield of individual crops
questions.explanation: (a) Overgrazing gives cheap feed and keeps grass short, but it destroys pasture, compacts soil and exposes it to erosion. (b) Bush burning clears land cheaply and kills pests while the ash supplies potash, but it destroys organic matter and soil organisms, exposes soil to erosion and pollutes air. (c) Crop rotation maintains fertility and controls pests and weeds, but it needs planning skill and is hard on small holdings. (d) Mixed cropping insures against crop failure and protects the soil, but crops compete for resources and the practice is hard to mechanize.

questions.stem: (a) Describe five ways by which crop nutrients are lost from the soil. [10 marks] (b) State six roles of organic fertilizers to the soil. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: (a) Any five described (2 marks each): leaching - nutrients dissolved and washed below the root zone; erosion - topsoil with nutrients carried away by water/wind; crop removal - nutrients taken away in harvested produce; burning - destroys organic matter and N and S volatilize; volatilization/denitrification - N lost as gas; continuous cropping - depletes nutrients; weed uptake
6 marks: (b) Any six (1 mark each): supplies plant nutrients (N, P, K and micronutrients); improves soil structure; increases water-holding capacity; improves aeration; increases cation exchange capacity/nutrient retention; encourages soil micro-organisms; buffers soil pH; reduces erosion
questions.explanation: (a) Nutrients are lost by leaching (washed beyond the root zone by percolating water), erosion (removal of the nutrient-rich topsoil), crop removal (nutrients exported in harvested produce), burning (organic matter destroyed and N and S lost as gases) and volatilization/denitrification of nitrogen. (b) Organic fertilizers supply nutrients, improve soil structure, raise water-holding capacity and aeration, increase the CEC and encourage beneficial soil organisms.

questions.stem: (a) Describe the following processes as methods of forest development: (i) regeneration; (ii) afforestation. [8 marks] (b) List eight benefits of forestry. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a)(i) Regeneration is the renewal of a forest after trees have been felled/destroyed, either naturally (from seeds, coppice shoots and seedlings left in the area) or artificially (by planting seedlings), with care of the young trees
4 marks: (a)(ii) Afforestation is the establishment of a forest on land that has not had forest before (or for a long time) by planting tree seedlings raised in a nursery, e.g. Gmelina, teak; including site preparation, planting and maintenance
8 marks: (b) Any eight (1 mark each): timber; fuel wood/charcoal; pulp for paper; habitat for wildlife/game; prevents erosion; protects watersheds; windbreak; medicinal plants; gums/resins/latex; food (fruits, bush meat, snails); regulates climate/rainfall; adds organic matter to soil; employment and revenue; tourism
questions.explanation: (a) Regeneration is the renewal of a forest after exploitation, either naturally from seeds and coppice shoots or artificially by planting, followed by tending. Afforestation is establishing a new forest by planting nursery-raised seedlings on land that was not under forest. (b) Forests provide timber, fuel wood, pulp, food, medicinal plants, gums and latex, wildlife habitats and employment, and they protect soil from erosion, act as windbreaks, and regulate climate.

questions.stem: Describe eight side effects of various preventive and control measures of pests. [16 marks]
questions.markingGuide: 16 marks: Any eight side effects described (2 marks each): chemicals kill beneficial insects (pollinators, natural enemies); pests develop resistance to pesticides; pesticide residues in food poison consumers; pollution of water bodies kills fish and aquatic life; toxic to farmers/applicators; pollution of soil and destruction of soil organisms; biological agents may become pests themselves; high cost of chemicals increases production cost; crop injury (phytotoxicity); bush burning destroys organic matter; resurgence of secondary pests; poisoning of livestock and wildlife
questions.explanation: Pesticides may kill beneficial organisms such as bees and natural enemies; pests develop resistance; residues in food poison consumers; run-off pollutes water and kills fish; chemicals harm the farmer's health; soil organisms are destroyed; introduced biological agents may become pests; and costs of control are high. Burning to control pests destroys organic matter, and some chemicals injure the crop itself.

questions.stem: (a) Explain the term lactation. [2 marks] (b) With the aid of a well labelled diagram, describe the structure of a farm animal mammary gland. [14 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Lactation is the secretion/production of milk by the mammary glands of a female animal after parturition, for a period (lactation period) until drying off
6 marks: (b) Diagram: correctly drawn udder/mammary gland showing and labelling alveoli, milk ducts, gland cistern, teat cistern, teat canal (streak canal), sphincter muscle (1 mark each label, max 6)
2 marks: The udder (of a cow) has four quarters, each a separate gland with its own teat, held by suspensory ligaments
2 marks: Milk is produced in the alveoli (lined with secretory cells and surrounded by myoepithelial cells and blood capillaries)
2 marks: Milk flows from the alveoli through small ducts into larger ducts and is stored in the gland cistern and the teat cistern
2 marks: It is released through the teat (streak) canal, which is closed by a sphincter muscle; milk let-down is controlled by oxytocin
questions.explanation: (a) Lactation is the production and secretion of milk by the mammary glands after parturition. (b) The cow's udder is divided into four independent quarters supported by ligaments, each with its own teat. Milk is secreted by secretory cells of the grape-like alveoli, flows through small and large ducts into the gland cistern and then the teat cistern, and leaves through the streak canal, which is kept closed by a sphincter muscle. The alveoli are surrounded by blood capillaries and muscle cells that contract under oxytocin to let down milk.

questions.stem: (a) Describe pig management under the following headings: (i) housing; [11 marks] (ii) creep feeding. [4 marks] (b) Mention one method of preventing anaemia in piglets. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Pigs can be housed in intensive (pens/sties), semi-intensive or extensive systems; the intensive system is most common
3 marks: Pen requirements: concrete floor sloping for drainage, easy to clean; walls about 1 - 1.2 m high; roof to protect against sun and rain; well ventilated
3 marks: Separate pens for boars, dry sows, farrowing sows (farrowing pen with guard rails/creep area to prevent overlying) and fatteners; adequate space per pig
3 marks: Provide feeding and watering troughs, a wallow or shower for cooling, drainage channels and footbath; site away from residential areas, on well-drained land with water supply
4 marks: (a)(ii) Creep feeding is the provision of a highly nutritious (high-protein) starter ration to piglets in a creep area that only they can enter, from about 2 weeks old before weaning; it supplements sow's milk, promotes rapid growth and eases weaning
1 mark: (b) Iron injection (iron dextran) to piglets in the first week, or provision of iron-rich soil/iron paste
questions.explanation: (a) Pigs are mostly kept intensively in pens with sloping, easily cleaned concrete floors, low walls, a roof, good ventilation and drainage, feeding and water troughs and a wallow or shower. Separate pens are provided for boars, dry sows, farrowing sows (with guard rails and a creep to prevent piglets being crushed) and growers. Creep feeding gives suckling piglets a high-protein starter ration in an enclosure the sow cannot enter, from about two weeks, to supplement milk and ease weaning. (b) Anaemia is prevented by injecting piglets with iron dextran (or giving iron-rich soil).

questions.stem: (a) Define (i) supply; (ii) demand. [4 marks] (b) List four factors each that affect: (i) supply; [4 marks] (ii) the price of an agricultural produce. [4 marks] (c) State one importance of the law of diminishing returns to farmers. [2 marks] (d) Explain the term income elasticity. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Supply is the quantity of a commodity that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price at a particular time
2 marks: (a)(ii) Demand is the quantity of a commodity that consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price at a particular time
4 marks: (b)(i) Any four (1 mark each): price of the commodity; cost of production/inputs; prices of related commodities; technology; weather/climate; government policy (taxes, subsidies); number of producers; pests and diseases
4 marks: (b)(ii) Any four (1 mark each): demand; supply; cost of production; government policy/price control; seasonality; perishability; quality of produce; transport cost
2 marks: (c) It helps the farmer to know the level at which to stop adding a variable input (e.g. fertilizer, labour) to a fixed input (land) so as to maximize profit and avoid waste
2 marks: (d) Income elasticity of demand is the degree of responsiveness of the quantity demanded of a commodity to a change in consumers' income (percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in income)
questions.explanation: (a) Supply is the quantity producers are willing to sell at a given price and time; demand is the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price and time. (b) Supply depends on price, cost of inputs, technology, weather and government policy. Price depends on demand and supply, cost of production, government policy, seasonality and quality. (c) The law of diminishing returns shows the farmer the point beyond which extra units of input yield less output, so he avoids wasteful use of inputs. (d) Income elasticity measures how quantity demanded responds to a change in income.

questions.stem: (a) Define Agricultural Extension. [2 marks] (b) State eight aims of Agricultural Extension. [8 marks] (c) List and explain two main types of extension methods. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Agricultural extension is an informal educational process that carries new farming knowledge and improved practices from research institutions to farmers (and their problems back to researchers) to improve production and living standards
8 marks: (b) Any eight (1 mark each): disseminate research findings to farmers; teach improved farming practices; increase farm output and income; improve rural living standards; feed back farmers' problems to researchers; help farmers obtain inputs and credit; organize farmers into co-operatives; develop rural leadership; encourage youths into farming; teach farm record keeping and marketing
3 marks: (c) Individual (personal) contact methods - extension agent meets farmers one-to-one through farm and home visits, office calls, telephone; effective but reaches few farmers
3 marks: (c) Group/mass methods - group methods such as demonstrations (method/result), field days, meetings, shows; mass methods such as radio, television, newspapers, posters, leaflets reach many farmers at once
questions.explanation: (a) Agricultural extension is the non-formal education of farmers, taking improved practices from research to the farmer and farmers' problems back to research. (b) Its aims include spreading research findings, teaching improved practices, raising output and income, improving rural welfare, linking farmers to inputs and credit, forming co-operatives, developing leadership and teaching record keeping. (c) Individual methods (farm and home visits, office calls) are personal and effective but reach few farmers; group and mass methods (demonstrations, field days, radio, television, posters) reach many farmers at once.

8 marks: Two contributions for each of the four areas (1 mark each), e.g. agronomy - improved varieties, better husbandry; animal science - improved breeds, better feeds/health; agricultural engineering - farm machines, irrigation/storage structures; agricultural economics/extension - farm planning/marketing, spreading innovations to farmers
questions.explanation: (a) Feed shortage causes slow growth, low milk/egg/meat yield, weight loss, poor fertility, greater disease susceptibility and even death. (b) Crop science develops high-yielding varieties and better husbandry; animal science develops improved breeds, feeds and health care; agricultural engineering provides machines, irrigation and storage structures; agricultural economics and extension improve farm management and marketing and carry innovations to farmers (also soil science, fisheries and forestry).

questions.stem: (a) State eight reasons why agriculture has not been fully mechanized in West Africa. [8 marks] (b) List four characteristics of each of (i) subsistence agriculture; [4 marks] (ii) commercial agriculture. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
8 marks: (a) Any eight (1 mark each): small/fragmented holdings; land tenure system; high cost of machines; lack of capital/credit; lack of skilled operators and mechanics; lack of spare parts; illiteracy of farmers; unfavourable topography/vegetation (stumps, hills); poor infrastructure (roads, electricity); cheap family labour; government policy inconsistency
4 marks: (b)(i) Subsistence, any four (1 mark each): small-scale production; production mainly for family consumption; use of crude tools; family labour; low capital; low yield; little or no use of improved inputs; mixed cropping
4 marks: (b)(ii) Commercial, any four (1 mark each): large-scale production; produce mainly for sale/profit; use of machines; hired/skilled labour; high capital investment; specialization (monocropping); use of improved inputs; high yields
questions.explanation: (a) Full mechanization is hindered by small fragmented holdings, the land tenure system, high cost of machines, lack of credit, shortage of skilled operators and spare parts, illiteracy, difficult terrain and vegetation, and poor infrastructure. (b) Subsistence agriculture is small-scale, uses family labour and crude tools, has low capital and low yields, and produces for home consumption. Commercial agriculture is large-scale, mechanized, uses hired labour, high capital and improved inputs, and produces for sale.

questions.stem: (a) Define land. [2 marks] (b) State the two major classification of land based on uses and give two examples in each case. [4 marks] (c) List six factors that influence the availability of land for agricultural production and explain two of the factors. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Land is the part of the earth's surface, including its soil, minerals, water and natural vegetation, available for use by man (a natural free gift)
2 marks: (b) Agricultural uses (1 mark), e.g. crop production and livestock grazing/fish farming/forestry (1 mark)
2 marks: (b) Non-agricultural uses (1 mark), e.g. building/industries and roads/mining/recreation (1 mark)
6 marks: (c) Any six factors listed (1 mark each): land tenure system; population pressure; topography; soil fertility/type; climate; industrialization/urbanization; government policy (e.g. land use act); erosion; cost of land
4 marks: Two factors explained (2 marks each), e.g. population pressure - increasing population uses more land for housing, reducing land for farming; land tenure - communal/inheritance systems fragment land and limit access
questions.explanation: (a) Land is the earth's surface with its soil, water, minerals and vegetation, a free gift of nature used for production. (b) Agricultural uses: crop farming, livestock grazing (also forestry, fish ponds). Non-agricultural uses: housing, industries, roads, mining. (c) Availability depends on the land tenure system, population pressure, topography, soil fertility, climate, urbanization and government policy. For example, rapid population growth takes land for houses and roads, and the inheritance tenure system fragments land into small plots.

questions.stem: (a) State three methods of irrigating a small nursery. [3 marks] (b) Enumerate three factors to be considered in the choice of each of: (i) surface irrigation method; (ii) subsurface irrigation method. [6 marks] (c) State two advantages of subsurface irrigation. [2 marks] (d) Enumerate five ways by which the build up of diseases could be reduced on an irrigated farm. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Any three (1 mark each): watering can; hose pipe; sprinkler; drip (trickle) irrigation; overhead perforated pipes
3 marks: (b)(i) Surface, any three (1 mark each): level/gentle topography; soil with moderate infiltration (not sandy); abundant water supply; type of crop; cost
3 marks: (b)(ii) Subsurface, any three (1 mark each): permeable top soil with an impervious layer beneath/high water table; level land; good quality (non-saline) water; capital for pipes; crop root depth
2 marks: (c) Any two (1 mark each): reduces evaporation losses; does not wet foliage, so fewer leaf diseases; does not interfere with field operations; reduces weed growth on the surface; no erosion
5 marks: (d) Any five (1 mark each): good drainage to prevent waterlogging; avoid over-irrigation; use clean water free of pathogens; control weeds that harbour pathogens; crop rotation; use resistant varieties; proper spacing; field sanitation (remove infected plants); regular spraying with pesticides; control snails/vectors
questions.explanation: (a) A nursery can be watered with a watering can, a hose, a sprinkler or drip lines. (b) Surface irrigation needs level land, soils of moderate infiltration and plenty of water; subsurface irrigation needs a permeable topsoil over an impervious layer, level land and good-quality water. (c) Subsurface irrigation reduces evaporation and keeps foliage dry, lowering leaf diseases. (d) Diseases can be reduced by good drainage, avoiding over-irrigation, using clean water, weed control, crop rotation, resistant varieties, proper spacing and field sanitation.

questions.stem: Discuss the following practices in crop production: (a) transplanting; [5 marks] (b) shading; [4 marks] (c) supplying/filling-in; [2 marks] (d) nursery. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Transplanting is the removal of seedlings from the nursery to the permanent field (or from one place to another)
3 marks: It is done when seedlings are strong (e.g. 4 - 6 weeks/3 - 4 leaves), preferably in the evening or on a cool/rainy day; water the nursery before lifting, lift with a ball of soil, plant at the same depth, water and shade afterwards
2 marks: (b) Shading is the provision of cover (palm fronds, sheds, shade trees) to protect young seedlings/plants from direct sunlight
2 marks: It reduces transpiration and scorching; temporary (e.g. plantain for cocoa) or permanent shade trees are used
2 marks: (c) Supplying (filling-in) is the replacement of seeds/seedlings that failed to germinate or died, to maintain the required plant population; done soon after germination
2 marks: (d) A nursery is a place where seeds are raised into seedlings before transplanting to the field (e.g. cocoa, tomato, oil palm)
3 marks: Nursery management: site near water, well drained, fertile soil; prepare beds or polybags; sow seeds, water, shade, weed, control pests and diseases; harden-off seedlings before transplanting
questions.explanation: Transplanting is moving seedlings from the nursery to the field at the right stage, preferably in cool weather, lifting them with a ball of earth, planting at the same depth and watering. Shading protects young plants from intense sunlight and reduces water loss, using sheds or temporary/permanent shade crops. Supplying is replacing seeds or seedlings that failed, soon after germination, to maintain plant population. A nursery is a specially prepared place for raising seedlings; it should be near water, well drained and fertile, and the seedlings are watered, shaded, weeded, protected and hardened off before transplanting.

questions.stem: (a) Define the terms budding and grafting. [4 marks] (b) List four materials required for budding. [2 marks] (c) Give two reasons why the improvement of crops by selection may not produce the desired results. [2 marks] (d) State four disadvantages of asexual reproduction and four advantages of sexual reproduction in crop plants. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Budding is the insertion of a bud (bud patch) of a desired plant (scion) into the stem of a rooted plant (stock) so that they unite and grow as one plant
2 marks: Grafting is the joining of a shoot/twig (scion) of a desired plant to a rooted plant (stock) so that they unite and grow as one plant
2 marks: (b) Any four (half a mark each, rounded): budding knife; budding tape/polythene strip; stock (seedling); bud wood (scion); grafting wax; secateurs; sharpening stone
2 marks: (c) Any two (1 mark each): the selected characters may be due to environment, not genes (not heritable); cross-pollination with inferior plants; variation may be too little; long time required; mutation
4 marks: (d) Disadvantages of asexual reproduction, any four (1 mark each): no new varieties/no variation; diseases are easily transmitted to offspring; bulky planting materials, difficult to store and transport; planting materials are perishable; plants may be short-lived/overcrowded
4 marks: (d) Advantages of sexual reproduction, any four (1 mark each): produces new varieties/variation; seeds are easy to store and transport; seeds can remain dormant/viable for long; fewer diseases transmitted; large numbers produced cheaply; hybrid vigour
questions.explanation: (a) Budding is the joining of a single bud from a desired plant onto a rootstock; grafting is the joining of a shoot (scion) onto a rootstock so that they grow as one. (b) Budding needs a budding knife, budding tape, a rootstock and bud wood. (c) Selection may fail because the selected traits were caused by environment rather than genes, or because cross-pollination with inferior plants occurs. (d) Asexual reproduction gives no variation, transmits diseases and uses bulky, perishable planting materials. Sexual reproduction produces variation and new varieties, and seeds are easy to store and transport and can stay viable for long.

questions.topic: Anatomy and physiology of farm animals
questions.stem: (a) Enumerate three major organs in each of the thoracic and abdominal cavities of farm animals. [6 marks] (b) State two functions of the nervous and one function of the reproductive systems. [3 marks] (c) Explain the importance of the following systems in farm animals: (i) circulatory system; [3 marks] (ii) respiratory system; [2 marks] (iii) digestive system. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Thoracic cavity, any three (1 mark each): heart; lungs; trachea; oesophagus; thymus
3 marks: (a) Abdominal cavity, any three (1 mark each): stomach; intestines; liver; kidneys; spleen; pancreas; reproductive organs (uterus/ovaries)
2 marks: (b) Nervous system, any two (1 mark each): coordinates body activities; receives and responds to stimuli; controls movement/reflexes; controls glandular secretion
1 mark: (b) Reproductive system: production of gametes / offspring (continuation of the species) / sex hormones
3 marks: (c)(i) Circulatory: transports nutrients and oxygen to tissues; removes waste products/CO2; transports hormones and antibodies; regulates body temperature
2 marks: (c)(ii) Respiratory: intake of oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide (gaseous exchange); helps temperature regulation (panting)
2 marks: (c)(iii) Digestive: breaks down food into simple absorbable forms; absorbs nutrients; eliminates undigested waste
questions.explanation: (a) Thoracic cavity: heart, lungs, trachea. Abdominal cavity: stomach, intestines, liver, kidneys. (b) The nervous system coordinates body activities and responds to stimuli; the reproductive system produces gametes and offspring. (c) The circulatory system transports nutrients, oxygen, hormones and wastes and regulates temperature; the respiratory system supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide; the digestive system breaks food down, absorbs nutrients and removes undigested waste.

questions.stem: (a) Describe the construction of a fish pond. [8 marks] (b) State eight measures necessary for the efficient operation of an egg incubator. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Select a site with reliable water supply, gentle slope and clay/loam soil that holds water; clear the site and survey/peg out the pond
2 marks: Excavate the pond to the desired depth (shallow end about 0.5 m to deep end 1.5 - 2 m) and build dykes/embankments from the clay soil, compacted to prevent seepage
2 marks: Install inlet and outlet (monk) pipes with screens/sieves to prevent escape of fish and entry of predators; provide spillway/overflow
2 marks: Lime the pond bottom, fertilize/manure to encourage plankton, plant grass on the dykes against erosion, fill with water, then stock with fingerlings
8 marks: (b) Any eight (1 mark each): maintain correct temperature (about 37.5 - 38 C / 99 - 100 F); maintain correct humidity (about 60 - 70 percent, higher at hatching); turn eggs regularly (at least 3 times daily) until day 18; ensure adequate ventilation; select clean, fertile, uncracked eggs of normal size; candle eggs to remove infertile ones; disinfect/fumigate the incubator; reliable power supply/standby generator; place eggs with the broad end up; stop turning 3 days before hatching; keep records
questions.explanation: (a) Choose a site with permanent water, gentle slope and water-retentive clay soil; clear and peg it out; excavate to a depth sloping from about 0.5 m to 1.5 - 2 m; build and compact dykes; fit inlet and outlet pipes with screens and a spillway; lime and fertilize the pond, grass the dykes, fill it with water and stock with fingerlings. (b) For an incubator: keep temperature at about 37.5 C and humidity at about 60 - 70 percent, turn eggs several times daily until day 18, ventilate well, set clean fertile eggs broad end up, candle and remove infertile eggs, disinfect the machine and ensure a reliable power supply.

questions.topic: Implications of demand and supply for agricultural production
questions.stem: (a) Discuss the effects of rural-urban migration on agricultural production. [3 marks] (b) Explain how: (i) demand affects agricultural production given that supply is constant; [2 marks] (ii) supply affects agricultural production when demand is constant. [2 marks] (c) State two effects of (i) demand on farmers' income when price is constant; [2 marks] (ii) supply on farmers' income when demand is constant. [2 marks] (d) State five roles expected of a farm manager in a farm enterprise. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Any three (1 mark each): shortage of farm labour; ageing farm population; reduced food production/food shortage; rise in cost of labour; abandonment of farmland; increased demand for food in towns
2 marks: (b)(i) An increase in demand raises price, encouraging farmers to produce more; a fall in demand lowers price and discourages production
2 marks: (b)(ii) An increase in supply lowers price and may discourage production; a fall in supply raises price, encouraging production
2 marks: (c)(i) Increase in demand increases quantity sold and so income rises; decrease in demand reduces income
2 marks: (c)(ii) Increase in supply lowers price and so may reduce farmers' income (demand being inelastic); decrease in supply raises price and income
5 marks: (d) Any five (1 mark each): planning farm operations; decision making; organization/coordination of resources; supervision of labour; record keeping; marketing of produce; evaluation/control of farm performance; procurement of inputs
questions.explanation: (a) Rural-urban migration drains young labour from farms, leaving an ageing farm population, raising labour costs and reducing food output while urban food demand rises. (b) With supply constant, higher demand raises prices and stimulates production, lower demand depresses it. With demand constant, higher supply lowers prices and may discourage production, while lower supply raises prices. (c) Rising demand at a constant price increases sales and income; rising supply with constant demand lowers prices and income. (d) A farm manager plans, takes decisions, organizes resources, supervises labour, keeps records and markets produce.

questions.stem: (a) State two methods of calculating depreciation of farm machines. [2 marks] (b) List four roles of capital in agricultural production. [4 marks] (c) Explain five major roles played by middlemen in the marketing of agricultural produce. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Any two (1 mark each): straight-line method; reducing (diminishing) balance method; sum-of-the-years' digits; revaluation method
4 marks: (b) Any four (1 mark each): purchase of land, machines and buildings; purchase of inputs (seeds, fertilizers, feeds); payment of labour; expansion of the farm; adoption of new technology; marketing and storage
10 marks: (c) Any five explained (2 marks each): assembling produce from scattered farmers; transportation to markets; storage to ensure all-year supply; grading and standardization; processing; financing farmers through advance payments; bearing risks; distribution in small quantities to consumers (retailing); providing market information to farmers; packaging
questions.explanation: (a) Depreciation may be calculated by the straight-line method or by the reducing-balance method. (b) Capital is used to buy land, machines and buildings, to buy inputs, to pay labour and to expand the business and adopt new technology. (c) Middlemen assemble produce from scattered farmers, transport it, store it for year-round supply, grade and process it, finance farmers through advance payments, bear market risks and distribute produce to consumers in convenient quantities.

questions.stem: (a) List six agro-based industries in your country and state the raw materials used in each industry. [6 marks] (b)(i) Discuss five problems normally experienced in the supply of raw materials to agro-based industries. [5 marks] (ii) Suggest five possible ways of solving the problems. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) Any six industries with their raw materials (1 mark each): textile mill - cotton; vegetable oil mill - oil palm/groundnut/soyabean; bakery/flour mill - wheat/maize/cassava; brewery - sorghum/maize/barley; sugar factory - sugar cane; tyre/rubber factory - latex; tannery/leather - hides and skins; feed mill - maize, soyabean, fish meal; cocoa/beverage factory - cocoa beans; saw mill/paper - timber/pulpwood; fruit juice/canning - fruits
5 marks: (b)(i) Any five problems (1 mark each): seasonal production/irregular supply; low output by small-scale farmers; poor quality/non-standard raw materials; poor transport/feeder roads; poor storage, leading to spoilage of perishable materials; high cost of raw materials; pests and diseases; competition with export/human consumption; inadequate funding of farmers
