questions.explanation: (a) Examples: textile mills use cotton; vegetable oil mills use palm fruit and groundnut; breweries use sorghum and maize; sugar factories use sugar cane; tyre factories use rubber latex; tanneries use hides and skins. (b) Problems include seasonal and irregular supply, low output from small farmers, poor quality, bad roads, poor storage and spoilage, and high prices. Solutions include industries running their own farms or out-grower schemes, giving farmers credit and inputs, improving roads and storage, contract farming at guaranteed prices, irrigation and better extension services.

questions.stem: (a) State two functions of each of the following implements: (i) sprayers; (ii) harrows; (iii) ploughs. [6 marks] (b) Outline six ways by which tractor-coupled implement may be maintained. [6 marks] (c) State four precautions to take when using a knapsack sprayer. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Sprayers: application of pesticides (insecticides, fungicides) and herbicides; application of foliar fertilizers/liquid chemicals; disinfecting animal houses
2 marks: (a)(ii) Harrows: break clods into fine tilth after ploughing; level the seedbed; incorporate manure/fertilizer; destroy/uproot weeds
2 marks: (a)(iii) Ploughs: cut, lift and turn (invert) the soil; bury weeds and crop residues; loosen soil for aeration and water infiltration
6 marks: (b) Any six (1 mark each): clean after use; grease/lubricate moving parts; tighten loose nuts and bolts; replace worn or broken parts; sharpen/adjust discs and blades; paint or oil metal parts to prevent rust; store under shelter; follow the manufacturer's manual
4 marks: (c) Any four (1 mark each): wear protective clothing (gloves, goggles, mask, boots); do not spray against the wind; mix chemicals in the correct proportion; do not eat, drink or smoke while spraying; check for leaks; wash the sprayer and yourself after use; store chemicals away from children
questions.explanation: (a) Sprayers apply pesticides and herbicides and foliar fertilizers; harrows break clods to fine tilth and level the seedbed; ploughs cut and turn the soil, burying weeds and loosening it. (b) Implements are maintained by cleaning after use, greasing moving parts, tightening bolts, replacing worn parts, sharpening discs and blades, painting/oiling to prevent rust and storing under shelter. (c) When using a knapsack sprayer wear protective clothing, spray with (not against) the wind, mix chemicals correctly, avoid eating or smoking, and wash the sprayer and yourself after use.

questions.topic: Types, composition and properties of soil
questions.stem: (a) Define (i) soil structure; (ii) soil profile; (iii) soil pH. [6 marks] (b) Discuss five ways in which soil structure influences crop production. [5 marks] (c) State five reasons for studying soil profile. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Soil structure is the arrangement or grouping of individual soil particles into aggregates (crumbs/peds)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Soil profile is the vertical section of the soil from the surface to the parent rock showing the different layers (horizons)
2 marks: (a)(iii) Soil pH is the measure of the degree of acidity or alkalinity of the soil (negative logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration)
5 marks: (b) Any five (1 mark each): affects soil aeration; affects water infiltration, retention and drainage; affects root penetration and development; affects activity of soil micro-organisms; affects ease of tillage/workability; affects resistance to erosion; affects nutrient availability
5 marks: (c) Any five (1 mark each): to know the depth of the soil/root zone; to know the texture and structure of horizons; to know the drainage condition (water table); to determine the fertility status/nutrient distribution; to know the type of crop to grow; to know the parent material and stage of soil formation; for soil classification; to plan irrigation, drainage and erosion control
questions.explanation: (a) Soil structure is the arrangement of soil particles into aggregates; a soil profile is a vertical section from the surface to parent rock showing horizons; soil pH measures acidity or alkalinity. (b) Structure affects aeration, water infiltration and retention, root penetration, microbial activity, ease of tillage and resistance to erosion. (c) A soil profile is studied to know the depth and texture of horizons, drainage conditions, fertility, suitable crops, parent material and classification of the soil.

questions.stem: (a) Describe each of the following methods of irrigation: (i) sprinkler; [2 marks] (ii) furrow; [2 marks] (iii) drip. [2 marks] (b) List five factors to consider when choosing an irrigation system. [5 marks] (c) State five problems associated with irrigation practices. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Sprinkler: water under pressure is pumped through pipes and sprayed into the air through rotating nozzles, falling on the crops like rain
2 marks: (a)(ii) Furrow: water is let into furrows (channels) between ridges or crop rows, from where it seeps sideways and downwards to the roots
2 marks: (a)(iii) Drip (trickle): water is delivered through small pipes/tubes with emitters, dripping slowly and directly to the base/root zone of each plant
5 marks: (b) Any five (1 mark each): source and amount of water available; topography/slope of the land; soil type (infiltration rate); type of crop; cost/capital available; climate (evaporation, wind); labour and technical know-how; water quality
5 marks: (c) Any five (1 mark each): salinization/alkalinity of soil; waterlogging; leaching of nutrients; spread of water-borne diseases (e.g. bilharzia, malaria); soil erosion; high cost of installation and maintenance; weed growth; silting of channels
questions.explanation: (a) Sprinkler irrigation sprays pressurised water over crops like rain; furrow irrigation runs water along channels between ridges to seep to the roots; drip irrigation delivers water slowly through emitters to each plant's root zone. (b) Choice depends on water availability, topography, soil type, crop, cost, climate and technical skill. (c) Irrigation can cause salinization, waterlogging, leaching, water-borne diseases, erosion, weed growth and high costs.

questions.stem: (a) Explain the following terms as used in crop production: (i) seed rate; [1 mark] (ii) plant density. [1 mark] (b) List five factors that determine the spacing of crops in the field. [5 marks] (c) If the number of yam setts required to plant 0.04 hectare is 215 and the weight of each yam sett is 0.80 kg. What is the seed rate per hectare in tonnes? [7 marks] (d) Name one pest and one disease of yam. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) Seed rate is the quantity (weight or number) of seeds/planting materials required to plant a unit area (e.g. one hectare)
1 mark: (a)(ii) Plant density (population) is the number of plants per unit area of land
5 marks: (b) Any five (1 mark each): type/variety of crop (size and growth habit); soil fertility; purpose of the crop; rainfall/moisture; method of cultivation (mechanized or manual); cropping system (sole or mixed); germination percentage/seed viability; light requirement
2 marks: (c) Weight of setts for 0.04 ha = 215 x 0.80 = 172 kg
2 marks: Seed rate per hectare = 172 / 0.04
1 mark: = 4,300 kg per hectare
2 marks: = 4.3 tonnes per hectare
1 mark: (d) Pest, e.g. yam beetle (or nematodes, mealybugs, rodents)
1 mark: Disease, e.g. yam anthracnose (or yam mosaic, dry rot, leaf spot)
questions.explanation: (a) Seed rate is the amount of planting material needed per unit area; plant density is the number of plants per unit area. (b) Spacing depends on the crop and variety, soil fertility, purpose of production, rainfall, method of cultivation, cropping system and seed viability. (c) 215 x 0.80 kg = 172 kg for 0.04 ha, so the seed rate = 172/0.04 = 4,300 kg/ha = 4.3 tonnes per hectare. (d) Pest: yam beetle; disease: yam anthracnose (or mosaic, dry rot).

questions.topic: Practical: Methods of propagation of horticultural plants
questions.stem: (a) List three advantages each of asexual and sexual methods of propagation. [6 marks] (b) Describe the steps involved in budding a citrus plant. [7 marks] (c) State three precautions in a budding operation. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Asexual, any three (1 mark each): offspring are true to type (identical to parent); faster maturity/early fruiting; propagates plants that do not produce viable seeds; combines desirable qualities of stock and scion; uniform crop
3 marks: (a) Sexual, any three (1 mark each): produces variation/new varieties; seeds are easy to store and transport; seeds remain viable for a long time; cheap and simple; produces many plants; fewer diseases transmitted
1 mark: (b) Raise a vigorous rootstock (e.g. rough lemon/sour orange) in the nursery until pencil-thick
2 marks: Make a T-shaped (or inverted T) cut in the bark of the stock about 15 - 25 cm above the ground and lift the bark flaps
2 marks: Remove a healthy bud (shield/patch with the bud) from the bud wood of the desired variety and insert it under the bark flaps
1 mark: Tie firmly with budding tape/polythene strip, leaving the bud exposed
1 mark: After 2 - 3 weeks remove the tape when the bud has taken (stays green); cut back the stock above the bud to force the bud to grow, remove shoots from the stock
3 marks: (c) Any three (1 mark each): use a sharp, clean (sterilized) knife; take buds from healthy, high-yielding mother plants; match the cambium of bud and stock; work quickly to prevent drying of the bud; tie firmly to exclude water and air; carry out budding when the bark peels easily (active growth)
questions.explanation: (a) Asexual propagation gives true-to-type, uniform plants that mature early and allows propagation of seedless plants; sexual propagation produces new varieties, and seeds are cheap, easy to store and transport and remain viable for long. (b) A vigorous rootstock is raised; a T-shaped cut is made in its bark; a bud shield cut from the desired variety is slipped under the bark flaps and tied firmly with tape, leaving the bud exposed; after 2 - 3 weeks the tape is removed and the stock is cut back above the bud to force it to grow. (c) Use a sharp, clean knife; select buds from healthy high-yielding parents; work quickly and tie firmly.

questions.stem: (a) Explain the term malnutrition. [2 marks] (b) State three symptoms of malnutrition in farm animals. [3 marks] (c) List five factors to consider in formulating rations for farm animals. [5 marks] (d) State two functions of each of the following nutrients in farm animals: (i) proteins; (ii) vitamins; (iii) minerals. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Malnutrition is a condition in an animal resulting from a diet deficient in one or more nutrients or with nutrients in wrong proportions (or excessive)
3 marks: (b) Any three (1 mark each): stunted growth/loss of weight; low productivity (milk, eggs); rough coat/loss of hair or feathers; deficiency diseases (e.g. rickets, anaemia); poor fertility; weakness/lethargy; pot belly
5 marks: (c) Any five (1 mark each): species/type of animal; age; purpose of production; physiological state (pregnancy, lactation); nutrient composition of feedstuffs; cost and availability of feedstuffs; palatability and digestibility; health status/body weight
2 marks: (d)(i) Proteins: body building/growth; repair of worn-out tissues; formation of enzymes, hormones and antibodies; production of milk, eggs, wool
2 marks: (d)(ii) Vitamins: regulate body processes/metabolism; prevent deficiency diseases; promote growth and fertility (e.g. vitamin A for vision, D for bones)
2 marks: (d)(iii) Minerals: formation of bones and teeth (Ca, P); formation of blood (Fe); egg shell formation; regulation of body fluids/nerve function; enzyme activation
questions.explanation: (a) Malnutrition is the condition caused by feeding a diet lacking in, or with wrong proportions of, essential nutrients. (b) Symptoms include stunted growth, weight loss, low production, rough coat and deficiency diseases. (c) Rations are formulated considering the species, age, purpose of production, physiological state, nutrient content, cost and availability, and palatability of feedstuffs. (d) Proteins build and repair tissues and form enzymes and antibodies; vitamins regulate metabolism and prevent deficiency diseases; minerals form bones, teeth and blood and regulate body fluids.

questions.stem: (a) Define the term disease in livestock production. [1 mark] (b) State the causal organism, prevention and two control measures of each of the following livestock diseases: (i) Newcastle disease; (ii) Anthrax; (iii) Rinderpest. [12 marks] (c) Name three predisposing factors of livestock diseases. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Disease is any condition that impairs the normal functioning (state of health) of an animal's body
1 mark: (b)(i) Newcastle disease: causal organism - virus (paramyxovirus)
1 mark: Prevention - vaccination of birds (e.g. with Lasota/Komarov vaccine)
2 marks: Control - isolate/destroy and burn sick birds; disinfect poultry houses and equipment; quarantine new birds; good hygiene
1 mark: (b)(ii) Anthrax: causal organism - bacterium (Bacillus anthracis)
1 mark: Prevention - vaccination
2 marks: Control - burn or bury carcasses deeply (never open them); quarantine; treat with antibiotics (penicillin); disinfect premises
1 mark: (b)(iii) Rinderpest: causal organism - virus
1 mark: Prevention - vaccination
2 marks: Control - isolate infected animals; slaughter and burn infected animals; quarantine and restrict cattle movement; disinfection
3 marks: (c) Any three (1 mark each): poor nutrition/malnutrition; poor housing/overcrowding; poor hygiene/sanitation; stress (e.g. transport, weather changes); age; parasite infestation; injuries; contaminated feed and water
questions.explanation: (a) Disease is any departure from the normal health of an animal that impairs its functioning. (b) Newcastle disease is caused by a virus; it is prevented by vaccination and controlled by destroying sick birds, disinfection and quarantine. Anthrax is caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis; it is prevented by vaccination and controlled by burning or deep burying carcasses, antibiotics and quarantine. Rinderpest is caused by a virus; it is prevented by vaccination and controlled by slaughtering infected animals, quarantine and restriction of cattle movement. (c) Predisposing factors include malnutrition, overcrowding, poor hygiene and stress.

questions.stem: (a) Write short notes on the following sources of farm finance: (i) agricultural banks; (ii) co-operative societies; (iii) savings and thrift societies; (iv) money lenders. [8 marks] (b) If a seed planter bought by a farmer at the cost of N120,000.00 is to last for 3 years, calculate the (i) annual depreciation if the value is assumed to fall by 1/5 of the original cost at the beginning of each year. [6 marks] (ii) salvage value of the seed planter at the end of the third year. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Agricultural banks are specialized government-owned banks that give loans to farmers (often at low interest and with long repayment periods), e.g. agricultural development banks
2 marks: (a)(ii) Co-operative societies pool members' resources and give loans to members at low interest; they can also obtain loans from banks on behalf of members
2 marks: (a)(iii) Savings and thrift societies (e.g. esusu/susu) are groups whose members contribute money regularly and take turns to collect the total, or borrow from the pool
2 marks: (a)(iv) Money lenders are private individuals who lend money readily without collateral but at very high (exorbitant) interest rates
2 marks: (b)(i) Annual depreciation = 1/5 x N120,000.00
4 marks: = N24,000.00 per year
1 mark: (b)(ii) Total depreciation over 3 years = 3 x N24,000.00 = N72,000.00
1 mark: Salvage value = N120,000.00 - N72,000.00 = N48,000.00
questions.explanation: (a) Agricultural banks are specialized banks that lend to farmers at relatively low interest and long terms; co-operative societies lend members pooled funds cheaply and borrow on their behalf; savings and thrift societies collect regular contributions which members take in turns or borrow from; money lenders give quick loans without collateral but at very high interest. (b) Annual depreciation = 1/5 x N120,000 = N24,000. After three years the value has fallen by N72,000, so the salvage value is N48,000.

questions.topic: Roles of government in agricultural development
questions.stem: (a) Mention five agricultural development programmes in West Africa. [5 marks] (b) State five general objectives of agricultural development programmes. [5 marks] (c) Suggest six reasons why agricultural extension programmes are ineffective in your country. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) Any five (1 mark each), e.g. Operation Feed the Nation (OFN); Green Revolution; Agricultural Development Projects (ADPs); River Basin Development Authorities; Farm Settlement Schemes; National Accelerated Food Production Programme (NAFPP); Directorate of Foods, Roads and Rural Infrastructure (DFRRI); National Fadama Development Project; Operation Feed Yourself (Ghana); Root and Tuber Expansion Programme
5 marks: (b) Any five (1 mark each): increase food production/self-sufficiency; increase farmers' income; provide raw materials for industries; create employment; improve rural infrastructure and living standards; reduce rural-urban migration; earn foreign exchange; encourage the use of improved technology
6 marks: (c) Any six (1 mark each): inadequate number of extension workers (poor agent-farmer ratio); poor funding; lack of transport/mobility; illiteracy and conservatism of farmers; poor remuneration and motivation of staff; poor roads to rural areas; inadequate teaching aids/equipment; language barrier; poor linkage with research institutes; policy inconsistency
questions.explanation: (a) Programmes include Operation Feed the Nation, the Green Revolution, Agricultural Development Projects, River Basin Development Authorities and farm settlement schemes (Operation Feed Yourself in Ghana). (b) Their objectives are to increase food production, raise farmers' incomes, supply raw materials, create jobs, improve rural infrastructure and reduce rural-urban migration. (c) Extension is ineffective because of too few agents, poor funding, lack of transport, farmers' illiteracy and conservatism, poor staff motivation, bad rural roads and weak links with research.

questions.stem: (a)(i) Define agriculture. [2 marks] (ii) List six branches of agriculture. [3 marks] (b) State five differences between commercial agriculture and subsistence agriculture. [5 marks] (c) State three merits and three demerits of using animal power on the farm. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Agriculture is the cultivation of crops and rearing of animals for man's use (food, clothing, shelter and raw materials), including processing and marketing of the products
3 marks: (a)(ii) Any six (half a mark each): crop science/agronomy; animal science; soil science; agricultural economics; agricultural extension; agricultural engineering; forestry; fisheries; crop protection; horticulture
5 marks: (b) Any five (1 mark each): commercial is large-scale, subsistence small-scale; commercial produces for sale/profit, subsistence for family consumption; commercial uses machines, subsistence crude tools; commercial uses hired labour, subsistence family labour; commercial requires high capital, subsistence little capital; commercial is specialized (monocropping), subsistence mixed cropping; commercial uses improved inputs and has high yields
3 marks: (c) Merits, any three (1 mark each): cheaper than tractors; available locally; dung used as manure; can work on small/uneven plots; animals can be sold or eaten at the end of their working life; does not need fuel or spare parts
3 marks: (c) Demerits, any three (1 mark each): slow; animals tire easily/limited hours of work; susceptible to diseases (e.g. trypanosomiasis); require feeding and care even when not working; need training; cannot be used for heavy operations
questions.explanation: (a) Agriculture is the art and science of cultivating crops and rearing animals for man's use, including processing and marketing; its branches include crop science, animal science, soil science, agricultural economics, extension, engineering, forestry and fisheries. (b) Commercial agriculture is large-scale, for profit, mechanized, uses hired labour, high capital and improved inputs and is specialized; subsistence agriculture is small-scale, for family consumption, uses crude tools, family labour and little capital. (c) Animal power is cheap, locally available, supplies manure and suits small plots; but it is slow, animals tire and fall sick, and they must be fed and trained.

questions.stem: (a)(i) Explain the term farm surveying. [2 marks] (ii) State four reasons why farm surveying is important. [4 marks] (b) Enumerate six problems facing agricultural development in West Africa. [6 marks] (c) List four factors that may affect the efficiency of draught animals. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Farm surveying is the measurement of farmland (distances, angles, elevations) to determine its size, shape and features and to prepare a map/plan of the farm
4 marks: (a)(ii) Any four (1 mark each): determines the area/size of the farm; helps in farm planning/siting of buildings, roads and fields; helps in planning irrigation, drainage and erosion control; settles boundary disputes; helps in valuation, sale or acquisition of land; provides maps/records
6 marks: (b) Any six (1 mark each): land tenure problems; inadequate capital/credit; poor infrastructure (roads, storage); pests and diseases; illiteracy of farmers; inadequate extension services; use of crude tools; poor marketing and price fluctuations; rural-urban migration (labour shortage); unfavourable weather/climate; inconsistent government policies
4 marks: (c) Any four (1 mark each): breed/size and strength of the animal; age; health; level of feeding/nutrition; training; working hours/climate (heat stress); type of implement and harness; terrain/soil condition
questions.explanation: (a) Farm surveying is measuring and mapping farmland to find its size, shape, slope and features. It is needed to know the farm area, plan the layout of buildings, roads and fields, design irrigation and drainage, settle boundary disputes and value the land. (b) Problems include land tenure, lack of capital, poor infrastructure, pests and diseases, illiteracy, inadequate extension, crude tools, poor marketing and rural-urban migration. (c) Draught animal efficiency depends on the breed and size, age, health, feeding, training and climate/working hours.

questions.topic: Types, composition and properties of soil
questions.stem: (a) Define the term soil. [2 marks] (b)(i) List the four components of soil. [2 marks] (ii) State the percentage of each component by volume. [2 marks] (c) Describe the process involved in making compost using the pit method under the following headings: (i) materials; [2 marks] (ii) preparation; [6 marks] (iii) storage. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Soil is the loose, weathered upper layer of the earth's crust, made up of mineral matter, organic matter, water and air, in which plants grow
2 marks: (b)(i) Mineral matter; organic matter; soil water; soil air (half a mark each)
2 marks: (b)(ii) Mineral matter 45%; organic matter 5%; water 25%; air 25% (half a mark each)
2 marks: (c)(i) Plant residues (grasses, leaves, crop wastes), animal dung/manure, wood ash, top soil, water (and a little fertilizer/lime)
2 marks: (c)(ii) Dig a pit (e.g. 1.5 m x 1.5 m x 1 m) in a shaded, well-drained site
2 marks: Arrange the materials in layers: plant materials, then animal dung, then a thin layer of top soil (and ash), repeated until the pit is filled; sprinkle water on each layer to keep it moist
2 marks: Cover the heap (with soil/leaves); turn the material every 2 - 3 weeks to aerate it and speed decomposition; insert a stick to check heat
2 marks: (c)(iii) Compost is ready in about 2 - 3 months (dark, crumbly, no bad smell); store it in a shaded, covered place (or bags) protected from sun and rain to prevent nutrient loss by leaching
questions.explanation: (a) Soil is the weathered surface layer of the earth's crust, made of mineral particles, organic matter, water and air, which supports plant growth. (b) Its components are mineral matter (about 45%), organic matter (5%), water (25%) and air (25%). (c) Materials are plant residues, animal dung, ash, topsoil and water. A pit is dug in a shaded, well-drained place and the materials are laid in alternating layers of plant matter, dung and soil, each watered, until the pit is full; the heap is covered and turned every few weeks. After 2 - 3 months the dark crumbly compost is stored under shade and cover to prevent nutrient loss.

questions.stem: (a) Define soil erosion. [2 marks] (b) List four factors that influence nutrient availability in the soil. [4 marks] (c) Explain two roles of each of the following factors in soil formation: (i) climate; (ii) living organisms; (iii) topography. [6 marks] (d) State four problems associated with overhead irrigation. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Soil erosion is the detachment and removal (washing or blowing away) of top soil from one place to another by agents such as water, wind and man/animals
4 marks: (b) Any four (1 mark each): soil pH; leaching; soil texture; organic matter content; soil micro-organisms; soil water/moisture; soil aeration; temperature; cation exchange capacity
2 marks: (c)(i) Climate: temperature changes cause expansion and contraction which break rocks; rainfall/water causes chemical weathering and moves weathered materials; wind erodes rocks
2 marks: (c)(ii) Living organisms: plant roots split rocks; organisms decompose organic matter to add humus; burrowing animals mix the soil; lichens/microbes produce acids that dissolve rocks
2 marks: (c)(iii) Topography: steep slopes lose soil by erosion so soils are shallow; low-lying areas receive deposits and are deep and often waterlogged; slope affects drainage and profile development
4 marks: (d) Any four (1 mark each): high cost of equipment and operation; high evaporation losses; uneven distribution in windy weather; wetting of foliage encourages diseases; requires reliable power/pressure; may cause soil crusting/erosion
questions.explanation: (a) Soil erosion is the removal of topsoil from one place to another by water, wind or human activity. (b) Nutrient availability depends on soil pH, leaching, texture, organic matter, micro-organisms and moisture. (c) Climate: temperature changes and rainfall cause physical and chemical weathering, and water moves weathered material. Living organisms: roots split rocks and organisms add humus and mix the soil. Topography: steep slopes give shallow, eroded soils, while valleys collect deep, often waterlogged deposits. (d) Overhead irrigation is costly, loses water by evaporation, distributes water unevenly in wind and wets foliage, encouraging diseases.

questions.stem: (a)(i) Define crop rotation. [2 marks] (ii) Design a four-year crop rotation system using yam, cassava, maize and groundnut. [8 marks] (b) State four reasons why weeds are difficult to control. [4 marks] (c) Mention two effects of diseases on crop production. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Crop rotation is the systematic growing of different crops in succession on the same piece of land over a number of years
2 marks: (a)(ii) Year 1: yam (heavy feeder, on fresh/fertile land)
2 marks: Year 2: maize (cereal)
2 marks: Year 3: groundnut (legume, to restore nitrogen)
2 marks: Year 4: cassava (can tolerate poorer soil); then the cycle repeats (or any sound arrangement of the four plots rotated over four years)
4 marks: (b) Any four (1 mark each): weeds produce large numbers of seeds; seeds remain dormant/viable in the soil for long; some have underground organs (rhizomes, tubers) that regenerate; they grow fast and compete strongly; seeds are easily dispersed by wind, water, animals; some resemble crops; some are resistant to herbicides; high cost of control
2 marks: (c) Any two (1 mark each): reduce yield; reduce quality and market value of produce; cause death of plants; increase cost of production; reduce storage life
questions.explanation: (a) Crop rotation is the growing of different crops in a planned sequence on the same land. A suitable four-year plan: year 1 yam (heavy feeder), year 2 maize, year 3 groundnut (legume to restore nitrogen), year 4 cassava (tolerates poorer soil), then repeat. (b) Weeds are hard to control because they produce many seeds that remain dormant for years, regenerate from rhizomes and tubers, grow fast and are widely dispersed. (c) Diseases reduce yield and quality and increase production costs.

4 marks: (c)(ii) Oestrogen, any four (1 mark each): development of female secondary sexual characteristics; induces heat (oestrus) behaviour; growth of the duct system of the mammary gland; prepares the uterus/thickens its lining; development of female reproductive organs; stimulates LH release for ovulation

2 marks: (d)(ii) Any two (1 mark each): lice; mites; fleas; ticks
questions.explanation: (a) New Zealand White, Californian, Chinchilla and Flemish Giant. (b) Oestrus detection ensures females are mated at the right time, improving conception and allowing planned breeding. (c) Androgens develop male organs and secondary sexual characteristics, stimulate sperm production and libido; oestrogen develops female characteristics, induces heat, develops the mammary duct system and prepares the uterus. questions.stem: (a) List four methods of identification in cattle production. questions.explanation: (a) Cattle are identified by ear tags, branding, ear notching and tattooing. questions.stem: (a) Define: (i) demand; (ii) price elasticity of demand. [4 marks] (b) Explain why the demand curve slopes downwards. [2 marks] (c) List four agents of agricultural marketing. [4 marks] (d) State two advantages and one disadvantage of each of the following agricultural extension teaching methods: (i) newspapers; (ii) television. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Demand is the quantity of a commodity that consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price at a particular time
2 marks: (a)(ii) Price elasticity of demand is the degree of responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the price of the commodity (percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price)
2 marks: (b) Because of the law of demand: at lower prices more is bought (consumers can afford more, new buyers enter, substitution effect, diminishing marginal utility), and at higher prices less is bought; price and quantity demanded are inversely related
4 marks: (c) Any four (1 mark each): producers/farmers; middlemen; wholesalers; retailers; co-operative societies; commodity boards/marketing boards; licensed buying agents; processors; exporters
2 marks: (d)(i) Newspapers - advantages: reach many farmers at once; information can be kept for future reference; relatively cheap
1 mark: Newspapers - disadvantage: useless to illiterate farmers / not readily available in rural areas / no immediate feedback
2 marks: (d)(ii) Television - advantages: combines sight and sound so steps can be seen; reaches many farmers; attractive and convincing
1 mark: Television - disadvantage: expensive; needs electricity; not available in most rural areas; no feedback
questions.explanation: (a) Demand is the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price and time; price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a price change. (b) The demand curve slopes downwards because price and quantity demanded are inversely related: at lower prices consumers buy more (income and substitution effects). (c) Marketing agents include farmers, middlemen, wholesalers, retailers, co-operatives and marketing boards. (d) Newspapers reach many readers cheaply and can be kept for reference but are useless to illiterate farmers. Television shows steps visually and reaches many, but it is expensive and needs electricity.

questions.stem: (a) List four factors that cause a change in supply of agricultural produce. [4 marks] (b) Distinguish between fixed cost and variable cost giving two examples in each case. [6 marks] (c) Explain the following agricultural extension teaching methods: (i) posters; (ii) field trips. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Any four (1 mark each): cost of production/inputs; technology; weather/climate; pests and diseases; government policy (taxes, subsidies); prices of related products; number of producers; producers' expectations
1 mark: (b) Fixed costs are costs that do not change with the level of output (incurred even when nothing is produced)
2 marks: Examples (1 mark each, any two): cost of land/rent; buildings; machinery/depreciation; salaries of permanent staff; insurance
1 mark: Variable costs change with the level of output (incurred only when production takes place)
2 marks: Examples (1 mark each, any two): seeds; fertilizers; feeds; agrochemicals; fuel; wages of casual labour
3 marks: (c)(i) Posters are large printed sheets with pictures and brief messages, displayed in public places (markets, offices, schools) to draw farmers' attention to new practices; they are cheap and reach many people but give limited information
3 marks: (c)(ii) Field trips are organized visits by groups of farmers to research stations, demonstration plots or successful farms to see new practices for themselves; they convince farmers by observation and allow discussion but are expensive and reach few
questions.explanation: (a) Supply changes with cost of inputs, technology, weather, pests and diseases, government policy and prices of related products. (b) Fixed costs do not vary with output (e.g. rent, machinery, permanent salaries); variable costs change with output (e.g. seeds, fertilizer, feed, casual labour). (c) Posters are pictorial notices displayed in public places to publicise improved practices. Field trips take farmers to research stations or model farms to observe new practices at first hand.

questions.stem: (a) Define the term land tenure system. [2 marks] (b) State two advantages of each of the following land tenure systems: (i) leasehold; (ii) freehold. [4 marks] (c) State two reasons why a disc plough is preferred to a mouldboard plough for land preparation in West Africa. [2 marks] (d)(i) Name four parts of a disc plough. questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Land tenure system is the system of land ownership, acquisition and use - the rights, rules and regulations governing how land is owned, held and used in a community
2 marks: (b)(i) Leasehold, any two (1 mark each): gives non-owners access to land; the lessee has security for the agreed period; owner earns rent; large areas may be leased for commercial farming
2 marks: (b)(ii) Freehold, any two (1 mark each): owner has absolute right to use, sell or transfer the land; encourages permanent crops and long-term investment; land can be used as collateral; no disputes over use
2 marks: (c) Any two (1 mark each): disc plough rolls over stumps, roots and stones without breaking; works better in hard, dry, sticky or stony soils common in West Africa; less draught/power required; less wear
4 marks: (d)(i) Any four (1 mark each): frame (beam); discs; disc bearings/hubs; scrapers; furrow wheel (rear wheel); hitch (three-point linkage/headstock); depth/land wheel; standards

questions.explanation: (a) A land tenure system is the set of rules governing ownership, acquisition and use of land. (b) Leasehold gives access to land for an agreed period and earns the owner rent; freehold gives absolute ownership, encourages permanent investment and the land can be used as collateral. (c) Disc ploughs ride over stumps and stones and work well in hard, dry or sticky soils. (d) Parts: frame (holds the parts together), discs (cut and turn the soil), scrapers (clean soil off the discs), furrow wheel (stabilizes the plough against side thrust), hitch (attaches it to the tractor).

2 marks: (a)(i) A straight fertilizer supplies only one primary nutrient (e.g. urea - N), while a compound (mixed) fertilizer supplies two or more primary nutrients (e.g. NPK 15:15:15)
4 marks: (a)(ii) Any four (1 mark each): urea; sulphate of ammonia; calcium ammonium nitrate; single/triple superphosphate; muriate of potash; NPK; sulphate of potash
3 marks: (b) Biotic, any three (1 mark each): pests; diseases/pathogens; weeds; predators; parasites; soil micro-organisms; man
3 marks: (b) Climatic, any three (1 mark each): rainfall; temperature; light/sunshine; relative humidity; wind
4 marks: (c) Any four (1 mark each): provides CO2 for photosynthesis; decomposition of organic matter returns nutrients to the soil; formation of humus improves soil structure; respiration releases energy; carbonic acid aids rock weathering/soil formation; maintains balance of CO2 and O2 in the atmosphere
questions.explanation: (a) Straight fertilizers supply one main nutrient (e.g. urea, muriate of potash); compound fertilizers supply two or more (e.g. NPK 15:15:15). Examples: urea, sulphate of ammonia, superphosphate, muriate of potash. (b) Biotic: pests, diseases, weeds. Climatic: rainfall, temperature, sunlight. (c) The carbon cycle supplies CO2 for photosynthesis, returns nutrients through decomposition, forms humus that improves soil structure and keeps atmospheric CO2 balanced.

questions.topic: Types, composition and properties of soil
questions.stem: (a) Explain the term soil. [2 marks] (b) List four characteristics of loamy soil. [4 marks] (c)(i) Draw an annotated diagram of the water cycle. [7 marks] (ii) List the three types of soil water. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Soil is the loose, weathered upper layer of the earth's crust, consisting of mineral matter, organic matter, water and air, which supports plant growth
4 marks: (b) Any four (1 mark each): a mixture of sand, silt and clay in good proportions; good water-holding capacity; good drainage and aeration; rich in humus/nutrients; easy to work; dark colour; good crumb structure
2 marks: (c)(i) Diagram shows the sea/water bodies and land surface with plants, the sun, clouds and arrows forming a cycle
2 marks: Annotation of evaporation (from water bodies) and transpiration (from plants) leading to water vapour
2 marks: Annotation of condensation forming clouds and precipitation (rainfall)
1 mark: Annotation of infiltration/percolation into soil and run-off/underground flow back to rivers and the sea
3 marks: (c)(ii) Gravitational water; capillary water; hygroscopic water (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) Soil is the weathered surface layer of the earth's crust made up of mineral matter, organic matter, water and air, in which plants grow. (b) Loamy soil has balanced proportions of sand, silt and clay, holds water well yet drains and aerates well, is rich in humus and is easy to work. (c) The water cycle: water evaporates from seas and rivers and transpires from plants; the vapour condenses into clouds; precipitation falls as rain; water infiltrates and percolates into the soil or runs off into rivers and back to the sea. The three types of soil water are gravitational, capillary and hygroscopic water.

questions.stem: (a) Give two examples each of crops that belong to the following crop groupings: (i) fibres; (ii) vegetables; (iii) tubers; (iv) oil crops; (v) legumes; (vi) cereals; (vii) tree fruits; (viii) beverages. [8 marks] (b) A vegetable crop is planted at a spacing of 40 cm x 40 cm on an 80 m x 40 m farmland. Calculate the expected plant population. [4 marks] (c) State four factors that should be considered in planning crop production. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) Fibres: cotton, jute, kenaf, sisal
1 mark: (ii) Vegetables: tomato, okro, pepper, amaranthus, cabbage
1 mark: (iii) Tubers: yam, cassava, cocoyam, sweet potato
1 mark: (iv) Oil crops: oil palm, groundnut, coconut, soyabean, sesame
1 mark: (v) Legumes: cowpea, groundnut, soyabean, pigeon pea
1 mark: (vi) Cereals: maize, rice, sorghum, millet
1 mark: (vii) Tree fruits: mango, orange, avocado pear, cashew
1 mark: (viii) Beverages: cocoa, coffee, tea, kola
1 mark: (b) Area of land = 80 m x 40 m = 3,200 m^2
1 mark: Area per plant = 0.4 m x 0.4 m = 0.16 m^2
2 marks: Plant population = 3,200 / 0.16 = 20,000 plants
4 marks: (c) Any four (1 mark each): soil type/fertility; climate (rainfall, temperature); availability of land; capital; labour; market demand/prices; availability of inputs (seeds, fertilizer); pests and diseases; technical know-how; type of crop
questions.explanation: (a) Fibres: cotton, jute; vegetables: tomato, okro; tubers: yam, cassava; oil crops: oil palm, groundnut; legumes: cowpea, soyabean; cereals: maize, rice; tree fruits: mango, orange; beverages: cocoa, coffee. (b) Area = 3,200 m^2; each plant occupies 0.16 m^2; plant population = 3,200/0.16 = 20,000 plants. (c) Planning depends on soil and climate, land, capital, labour, market demand, availability of inputs and pests and diseases.

questions.stem: (a) Explain each of the following terms as used in crop production: (i) grafting; (ii) thinning; (iii) staking. [6 marks] (b) State two reasons for adopting each of the crop production activities listed in 6(a). [6 marks] (c) Mention the botanical names of two species of yam. [2 marks] (d) State two uses of ginger. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Grafting is the joining of a shoot (scion) from a desired plant to a rooted plant (stock) so that they unite and grow as one plant
2 marks: (a)(ii) Thinning is the removal of excess seedlings from a stand/row to leave the required number of healthy plants at the correct spacing
2 marks: (a)(iii) Staking is the provision of sticks/poles to support climbing or weak-stemmed crops such as yam and tomato
2 marks: (b) Grafting, any two (1 mark each): combines good qualities of stock and scion; early fruiting; propagates seedless/difficult plants; produces true-to-type plants; disease resistance from stock
2 marks: (b) Thinning, any two (1 mark each): reduces competition for nutrients, water and light; allows remaining plants to grow vigorously; maintains optimum plant population; reduces pest/disease spread
2 marks: (b) Staking, any two (1 mark each): exposes leaves to sunlight for photosynthesis; prevents fruits from touching the soil and rotting; increases yield; eases weeding, spraying and harvesting; prevents lodging
2 marks: (c) Any two (1 mark each): Dioscorea rotundata (white yam); Dioscorea alata (water yam); Dioscorea cayenensis (yellow yam); Dioscorea dumetorum (bitter yam); Dioscorea bulbifera (aerial yam)
2 marks: (d) Any two (1 mark each): spice for flavouring food; medicinal purposes; making beverages/drinks (ginger beer, tea); export/income; cosmetics/perfume
questions.explanation: (a) Grafting joins a scion to a rootstock so they grow as one; thinning removes excess seedlings to the required number; staking supports climbing or weak plants with poles. (b) Grafting gives early, true-to-type fruiting and combines good stock and scion qualities; thinning reduces competition and ensures vigorous growth; staking exposes leaves to light, keeps fruits off the soil and raises yield. (c) Dioscorea rotundata (white yam) and Dioscorea alata (water yam). (d) Ginger is used as a spice and in medicine (and for beverages).

questions.stem: (a)(i) Explain the terms line breeding and inbreeding as used in animal improvement. [4 marks] (ii) State three advantages and three disadvantages of inbreeding. [6 marks] (b) State four factors that determine the amount of water required by farm animals. [4 marks] (c) Give four sources of calcium in the diet of livestock. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Line breeding is a mild form of inbreeding in which animals that are distantly related but descended from one outstanding ancestor are mated, to keep that ancestor's qualities in the line
2 marks: Inbreeding is the mating of closely related animals, e.g. sire to daughter, brother to sister
3 marks: (a)(ii) Advantages, any three (1 mark each): fixes desirable traits; produces uniform/pure lines; exposes and eliminates undesirable recessive genes; helps develop new breeds; useful for progeny testing
3 marks: (a)(ii) Disadvantages, any three (1 mark each): inbreeding depression (reduced vigour, growth, fertility); brings out undesirable recessive traits/abnormalities; higher mortality; reduced resistance to diseases; reduced variation
4 marks: (b) Any four (1 mark each): species/type of animal; size/body weight; age; physiological state (lactation, pregnancy); type of feed (dry or succulent); environmental temperature/humidity; level of activity; health status
2 marks: (c) Any four (half a mark each): bone meal; oyster shell; limestone/calcium carbonate; dicalcium phosphate; legumes/green forage; fish meal; milk
questions.explanation: (a) Line breeding mates distantly related animals to concentrate the genes of an outstanding ancestor; inbreeding mates closely related animals such as sire and daughter. Inbreeding fixes desirable traits, produces uniform lines and exposes harmful recessive genes for elimination, but it can cause inbreeding depression, abnormalities, low fertility and reduced disease resistance. (b) Water needs depend on species, body size, age, physiological state, type of feed, environmental temperature and activity. (c) Calcium sources: bone meal, oyster shell, limestone and leguminous forage.

questions.stem: (a) State three characteristics of each of the following classes of animal feedstuffs: (i) roughage; (ii) basal feeds; (iii) concentrates. [9 marks] (b) Enumerate four factors that should be considered in selecting a site for the construction of a fish pond. [4 marks] (c) State three preventive and control measures of diseases in farm animals. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Roughage, any three (1 mark each): high crude fibre content (above 18%); bulky; low digestibility; low in energy/nutrients; suited to ruminants, e.g. hay, silage, grasses, straw
3 marks: (a)(ii) Basal feeds, any three (1 mark each): rich in carbohydrate (energy); low in protein (below 20%); low fibre; form the bulk of the ration; e.g. maize, sorghum, cassava, wheat offal
3 marks: (a)(iii) Concentrates, any three (1 mark each): high in protein and/or energy; low in fibre; highly digestible; less bulky; expensive; e.g. groundnut cake, soyabean meal, fish meal, blood meal
4 marks: (b) Any four (1 mark each): reliable source of water; soil type (clay/loam that holds water); topography (gentle slope); freedom from flooding; nearness to market; accessibility/security; absence of pollution; cost of land
3 marks: (c) Any three (1 mark each): vaccination; good sanitation/hygiene; quarantine of new or sick animals; isolation of sick animals; proper feeding; deworming and dipping/spraying against ecto-parasites; treatment with drugs/antibiotics; good housing; proper disposal of dead animals
questions.explanation: (a) Roughages are bulky, high in fibre and low in digestibility and nutrients (e.g. hay, grasses). Basal feeds are high in energy (carbohydrate), low in protein and fibre and form the bulk of the ration (e.g. maize, cassava). Concentrates are rich in protein and/or energy, low in fibre, highly digestible and expensive (e.g. groundnut cake, fish meal). (b) A fish pond site needs a reliable water supply, water-retentive soil, gentle slope, freedom from flooding and pollution, and good access and security. (c) Diseases are prevented and controlled by vaccination, good hygiene, quarantine and isolation, proper feeding, deworming and treating sick animals.

questions.stem: (a) Describe each of the following farm records: (i) farm diary; (ii) farm inventory; (iii) balance sheet. [9 marks] (b) Outline three factors that can affect the price of rice. [3 marks] (c) Explain the following agricultural extension teaching methods: (i) print media; (ii) film shows. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) A farm diary is a daily record of all activities/operations carried out on the farm (e.g. dates of planting, fertilizer application, vaccination, harvesting) and events such as rainfall or visitors
3 marks: (a)(ii) A farm inventory is a record of all the assets (physical properties) owned by the farm - land, buildings, machines, tools, livestock, stock of produce - with their values, at a particular time
3 marks: (a)(iii) A balance sheet is a financial statement that shows the assets and liabilities of the farm business at a particular date, indicating its net worth (financial position)
3 marks: (b) Any three (1 mark each): supply of rice (harvest/season); demand for rice; cost of production; importation of rice/government policy (tariffs); cost of transport; quality of rice; storage facilities; prices of substitutes
2 marks: (c)(i) Print media uses written materials such as newspapers, magazines, leaflets, bulletins, posters and handbills to spread agricultural information to many farmers; useful only to literate farmers
2 marks: (c)(ii) Film shows use films/videos projected to groups of farmers (e.g. mobile cinema) to show new practices visually; they combine sight and sound and attract attention
questions.explanation: (a) A farm diary is a day-to-day record of farm operations and events; a farm inventory is a list of all farm assets and their values at a given time; a balance sheet shows the farm's assets and liabilities at a particular date and therefore its net worth. (b) The price of rice depends on supply, demand, cost of production, importation/government policy and transport costs. (c) Print media (newspapers, leaflets, posters) spread written information to literate farmers; film shows use projected films to demonstrate practices visually to groups of farmers.

questions.stem: (a) Explain the following terms as used in agricultural production: (i) hired labour; (ii) fixed capital; (iii) management. [9 marks] (b) Give three reasons why the prices of most agricultural produce are unstable in West Africa. [3 marks] (c) Describe the following agricultural extension teaching methods: (i) field day; (ii) agricultural shows. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Hired labour is labour employed and paid wages (daily, weekly or monthly, or per task) for work on the farm, as opposed to family labour; it may be skilled or unskilled, permanent or casual
3 marks: (a)(ii) Fixed capital consists of durable assets used in production over a long period and not used up in one production cycle, e.g. land improvements, buildings, tractors, machinery, irrigation equipment
3 marks: (a)(iii) Management (entrepreneurship) is the factor that organizes and coordinates the other factors of production (land, labour, capital), takes decisions and bears the risks, with profit as its reward
3 marks: (b) Any three (1 mark each): seasonal production (glut at harvest, scarcity off-season); perishability of produce; lack of storage and processing facilities; weather-dependent output; inelastic demand; poor transport/marketing; activities of middlemen; lack of price control
2 marks: (c)(i) A field day is a day when farmers are invited to a demonstration plot, research station or farm to see the results of new practices and discuss them with extension agents and researchers
2 marks: (c)(ii) Agricultural shows are exhibitions/fairs where improved crops, animals, machines and products are displayed (often with competitions and prizes) to educate and motivate farmers
questions.explanation: (a) Hired labour is paid labour employed on the farm; fixed capital is durable assets such as buildings and machines used over many production cycles; management organizes the other factors, takes decisions and bears risks, earning profit. (b) Prices are unstable because production is seasonal, produce is perishable, storage and processing are inadequate, output depends on weather and marketing is poor. (c) A field day brings farmers to a farm or research station to observe and discuss results of new practices; agricultural shows exhibit improved crops, animals and equipment, often with competitions, to educate and motivate farmers.
